45 kg (governed by the weakest component in the suspension chain)
131.7 kg (the average of the three ratings)
explanation: A mount's published rating applies only to the bracket itself; every bolt, pipe, coupling, and anchor has its own rating, and the weakest part determines the maximum safe load of the entire assembly.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 7, pp. 158-160

topic: Prohibition on Drilling Steel I-Beams / RSJs
prompt: What is the mandatory rule when attaching an AV substructure or steel-channel strut to a structural steel I-beam (Rolled Steel Joist / Universal Beam)?
choices: Drill 20 mm holes through the bottom flange of the I-beam every 300 mm
Torch-cut a notch into the vertical web of the I-beam to recess the pipe
Shoot drywall screws into the steel flange with an impact driver
Never drill into a structural steel I-beam; use rated beam clamps (or approved welding by a certified welder) to attach steel-channel strut
explanation: Drilling into a structural steel I-beam (RSJ) weakens its load-bearing integrity and is strictly prohibited; always clamp or weld steel-channel strut (such as Unistrut) to the beam.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 7, pp. 169-170

topic: Continuous Black-Iron Pipe versus Coupled Pipe Weak Points
prompt: Why should an installer cut a single continuous length of black-iron pipe for a ceiling projector drop rather than joining two shorter pipes with a threaded coupling?
choices: Every threaded pipe coupling introduces two additional mechanical weak points and potential unscrewing hazards in the suspension column
Couplings block the flow of cooling water through the projector pipe
Couplings increase the optical throw ratio of the projector lens
Black-iron pipe cannot be threaded on a job site
explanation: Joining two pipes with a coupling creates two new mechanical weak points; installers should use a single continuous length of scheduled black-iron pipe and lock all threaded junctions with setscrews or through-bolts.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 7, pp. 164-165

topic: Threaded Rod Vertical-Only Load Restriction
prompt: For which type of load orientation is threaded rod (all-thread) rated and permitted in AV substructure rigging?
choices: Horizontal cantilevered wall booms supporting 50 kg speakers
Vertical suspension loads only (in axial tension)
Diagonal earthquake pry bars
Freestanding floor pedestals in high-traffic corridors
explanation: Threaded rod (all-thread) has high axial tensile strength but bends easily under side loads; it must be used only for vertical suspension mounts.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 7, p. 164

topic: Cantilevered Wall Bracket Top-Bolt Pull-Out Stress
prompt: When a heavy PTZ camera or articulated flat-panel arm is mounted on a vertical wall bracket, which fasteners experience the greatest pull-out leverage stress?
choices: Only the center decorative cover screw
The bottom row of bolts, which only experience compressive force
The top row of mounting bolts/anchors, because the cantilevered bracket acts like a pry bar pulling the top edge away from the wall
None of the bolts experience pull-out force on a vertical wall
explanation: Gravity acting on a cantilevered wall bracket creates a lever moment that tries to pry the top of the bracket away from the wall, placing maximum pull-out stress on the top bolts and anchors.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 7, pp. 159-161

topic: Concrete Expansion Anchor Hole Cleaning Requirement
prompt: After drilling a hole into a solid concrete slab with a rotary hammer drill to install a mechanical or chemical expansion anchor, what step is critical before inserting the anchor?
choices: Fill the hole with cable pulling lubricant so the anchor slides in easily
Enlarge the mouth of the hole by wobbling the spinning drill bit in circles
Drive a wooden dowel into the hole alongside the steel anchor
Blow or vacuum all pulverized concrete dust out of the hole so the anchor grips solid masonry rather than loose powder
explanation: Concrete dust left inside a drilled hole acts as a dry lubricant and prevents mechanical wedges or chemical epoxies from bonding to the concrete wall, drastically reducing pull-out strength.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 7, pp. 171-172

topic: Concrete Ceiling Strut Bridge Layout for 70 kg Projector
prompt: When laying out a two-tier steel-channel strut (Unistrut) suspension grid on a concrete slab for a 70 kg (155 lb) projector, what is the minimum number of rated concrete anchors required on each upper 1.2 m (48 in.) strut rail?
choices: At least 3 mounting points per upper strut rail using ISO 8.8 or SAE Grade 5 hardware
A single toggle bolt in the center of each rail
Two plastic drywall plugs per rail
No anchors; the upper strut rails are held up by friction against the ceiling tiles
explanation: In the standard heavy-projector concrete ceiling suspension layout, each of the two parallel 1.2 m (48 in.) upper steel-channel strut rails is anchored to the slab at a minimum of three points using ISO 8.8 / Grade 5 fasteners.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 7, pp. 173-176

topic: Safe Drop-Ceiling Tile Opening Technique
prompt: When lifting an acoustic ceiling tile for the first time to inspect or mount overhead rigging, why should the installer wear safety glasses and tilt the tile away from their face?
choices: To keep ceiling light from reflecting off the safety glasses
So any loose ceiling debris, metal shavings, old wire scraps, or abandoned tools resting on top of the tile slide away rather than falling into the installer's face and eyes
To prevent air pressure from lifting the floor carpet
Because acoustic tiles are magnetically attracted to hard hats
explanation: The top of a drop-ceiling tile often holds accumulated construction debris, metal shavings, or loose hardware left by other trades; tilting the tile away while wearing eye protection prevents facial and eye injuries.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 7, pp. 170-171

topic: NEC Maximum Conduit Fill Percentages (1, 2, and 3+ Cables)
prompt: What are the standard maximum permissible conduit cross-sectional fill percentages for pulling 1 cable, 2 cables, and 3 or more cables?
choices: 100% for 1 cable, 75% for 2 cables, and 50% for 3+ cables
25% for 1 cable, 50% for 2 cables, and 75% for 3+ cables
53% for 1 cable, 31% for 2 cables, and 40% for 3 or more cables
40% regardless of whether 1, 2, or 10 cables are pulled
explanation: Standard NEC/AHJ conduit fill limits allow 53% fill for a single cable, drop to 31% for two cables (which form a rigid flat profile that binds easily), and allow 40% fill for three or more cables.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, pp. 130-131; Appendix A, p. 431

topic: Staggered Cable Snout Construction Rules
prompt: When building a staggered cable snout to pull a multi-cable bundle through a raceway, which cable is placed in the lead position and how far apart are the remaining cables staggered?
choices: The thinnest optical fiber is placed in front, with all other cables taped flush at the exact same tip
The shortest coax cable is placed in front, with 1 meter gaps between cables
A bare copper ground wire is tied in a square knot at the tip without tape

The longest and strongest (largest gauge) cable is placed in the lead, with each subsequent cable staggered 75–100 mm (3–4 in.) behind and secured with a slip knot 600 mm (2 ft) back, half-hitches, and smooth flexible tape
explanation: A proper cable snout places the longest, heaviest-gauge cable in the lead, staggers remaining cables in 75–100 mm (3–4 in.) steps, anchors the pull string with a slip knot 600 mm (2 ft) from the tip plus 3–4 half-hitches, and wraps stretched tape into a smooth, flexible cone.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, pp. 136-138

topic: No Cable Left Behind 4-Step Cable Pulling and Labeling Workflow
prompt: Order the four steps of the 'No Cable Left Behind' temporary cable labeling and pulling workflow in the exact sequence performed in the field.
steps: Apply a matching temporary ID label ~600 mm (2 ft) from the leading end of the cable AND onto the supply spool
Pull the cable along the designated pathway to its destination without exceeding tension or bend-radius limits
Transfer the ID label from the supply spool to the trailing end of the cable (~600 mm / 2 ft from the cut point)
Cut the cable free from the supply spool
explanation: Labeling both the leading end and the spool first, pulling the run, transferring the spool label to the trailing end before cutting, and then cutting the cable ensures no unlabeled cable end is ever orphaned.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, pp. 134-136

topic: Temporary Cable Label Placement Distance from End
prompt: Why should temporary write-on cable labels be applied approximately 600 mm (2 ft) back from each end of the cable prior to building the pulling snout?
choices: So the labels are not covered by the snout tape, torn off during pulling, or cut off when stripping the cable ends for termination
Because permanent AVIXA F501.01 labels must be 600 mm long
To increase the capacitive reactance of the twisted pairs
So the labels remain hidden inside the wall conduit forever
explanation: Placing temporary labels ~600 mm (2 ft) from the cable ends keeps them clear of the tapered snout tape and ensures they survive cutting and jacket stripping at termination time.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, pp. 134-135

topic: Maximum Pulling Tension for 24 AWG Microphone Cable
prompt: A balanced microphone cable contains two 24 AWG copper signal conductors (rated at 1.8 kg / 4 lb max pulling tension each) and one 24 AWG shield drain wire (1.8 kg / 4 lb). What is the maximum total pulling tension for this single cable?
choices: 1.8 kg (4 lb)
explanation: Total allowable pulling tension equals the sum of each conductor's tension limit: 1.8 kg + 1.8 kg + 1.8 kg = 5.4 kg (4 lb + 4 lb + 4 lb = 12 lb).
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, pp. 137-138, 151

topic: Maximum Pulling Tension for 22 AWG Microphone Cable
prompt: If an installer pulls a heavier-gauge microphone cable consisting of two 22 AWG signal conductors (3 kg / 7 lb limit each) and one 24 AWG drain wire (1.8 kg / 4 lb limit), what is the approximate maximum safe pulling tension?
choices: 3.0 kg (7 lb)
explanation: Summing the two 22 AWG conductors (3 kg + 3 kg) and the 24 AWG drain wire (1.8 kg) yields 7.8 kg (~8 kg or 18 lb) of maximum safe pulling tension.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, pp. 137-138

topic: Overhead Cable Support with Bridle Rings and J-Hooks
prompt: When routing horizontal AV cables above a suspended drop ceiling where no enclosed conduit or cable tray exists, how must the cables be supported?
choices: Lay the cables directly on top of the acoustic drop-ceiling tiles
Wrap the cables around fire-sprinkler pipes and electrical EMT conduits
Drape the cables across fluorescent light fixtures
Suspend the cables from the primary building structure (bar joists/deck) using J-hooks or bridle rings spaced every 1.2–1.5 m (4–5 ft)
explanation: Cables must never rest on ceiling tiles or hang from sprinkler pipes or ceiling grid wires; they must be supported every 1.2–1.5 m (4–5 ft) on J-hooks, bridle rings, or cable trays anchored to the building structure.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, pp. 129-130

topic: Pneumatic Mouse / Rat Kit for Long Feeder Conduits
prompt: Which specialized tool uses a vacuum or compressed air to blow a foam cylinder/ball carrying a pull line through a sealed metallic feeder conduit longer than 60 m (200 ft)?
choices: A mouse or rat kit
An optical time-domain reflectometer (OTDR)
A rotary coaxial stripping cassette
A piezo tweeter
explanation: For long, continuous sealed conduits exceeding 60 m (200 ft) without open intermediate pull boxes, a pneumatic 'mouse' or 'rat' foam piston is blown or vacuumed through the conduit to pull the initial line.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, pp. 133-134

topic: Pulling Optical Fiber by Kevlar Aramid Strength Member
prompt: When pulling fiber-optic cable through a conduit or raceway, to which part of the cable must the pulling grip or tension line be attached?
choices: Directly to the 9-micron glass core
To the internal Kevlar aramid yarn strength members (never the glass fiber core alone)
To the fragile LC ceramic ferrules
To a soldered copper drain wire inside the cladding
explanation: Optical fiber cables contain Kevlar aramid yarn (or fiberglass rod) strength members specifically designed to bear pulling tension so the delicate glass core and cladding are never stretched.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, pp. 116-119, 137

topic: Crossing AC Power and Signal Cables at 90 Degrees
prompt: When routing low-voltage audio, video, or data cables near AC mains power lines in a ceiling or rack, what rule must be followed to minimize 50/60 Hz inductive coupling?
choices: Twist the audio cables tightly around the AC mains conduit for 10 meters
Strip the outer shield off the microphone cable where it passes the breaker panel
Keep signal cables physically separated from parallel AC lines and cross them only at 90-degree right angles when a crossing is unavoidable
Connect the audio shield to the neutral busbar of the lighting dimmer pack
explanation: Alternating magnetic fields around AC mains conductors induce 50/60 Hz hum into parallel signal cables; maintain physical separation and cross AC power lines strictly at a 90-degree angle.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, p. 129; Chapter 8, p. 198

topic: Solid versus Stranded Conductors for Infrastructure Pulling
prompt: Why is solid-core copper conductor preferred over stranded conductor for permanent in-wall and conduit infrastructure pulls, whereas stranded conductor is preferred for patch cords and stage cables?
choices: Solid-core wire has unlimited flex life for coiling on stage floors
Stranded wire is cheaper and seats more reliably in solid-only punch-down blocks
Solid-core wire cannot conduct DC phantom power

Solid-core wire costs less, exhibits lower high-frequency skin-effect attenuation, and withstands higher tensile strain during pulling, whereas stranded wire offers high flex life for repeated bending
explanation: Solid conductors handle greater tensile pulling strain and have lower cost and attenuation for fixed infrastructure, while stranded conductors provide high flex life for movable patch cables and live events.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, pp. 107-109

topic: Riser-Rated Cable Requirement for Vertical Inter-Floor Shafts
prompt: When pulling backbone AV cables vertically from the 2nd floor to the 5th floor through a building riser shaft (non-plenum), what specialized cable feature is required?
choices: Riser-rated fire-retardant jacketing (such as CMR/OFNR) with internal load-bearing strength members to support the vertical weight of the cable
Submersible marine-grade lead armor
Uninsulated bare copper braid
Standard household lamp cord (zip cord)
explanation: Vertical runs between floors require riser-rated cable (preventing flame propagation from floor to floor) equipped with internal strength members so the cable's own hanging weight does not stretch the conductors.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, pp. 111-112

topic: Minimum Bend Radius Protection During Pulling
prompt: What physical damage occurs if an installer pulls a coaxial, Category 6A, or fiber-optic cable tightly around a sharp 90-degree metal corner that violates the cable's minimum bend radius?
choices: The cable's outer jacket changes color from blue to yellow
In copper coax/UTP, crushing the dielectric alters characteristic impedance and causes signal reflections/return loss; in optical fiber, it causes macro-bending light loss or cracks the glass core
The cable automatically increases its bandwidth from 1 Gbps to 10 Gbps
The DC resistance drops to zero ohms
explanation: Exceeding minimum bend radius deforms the dielectric spacing and pair geometry in copper cables (altering characteristic impedance and causing reflections) and fractures or leaks light from optical fiber cores.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, pp. 109, 118, 138

topic: Cleaning Pulling Lubricant Off Exposed Service Loops
prompt: When approved cable-pulling lubricant is used to ease friction on a long conduit run containing multiple bends, why must the installer wipe excess lubricant off the exposed service loops at the rack and wall box?
choices: Pulling lubricant is highly explosive when exposed to room light
Lubricant converts balanced audio into unbalanced audio
Residual lubricant on exposed jackets attracts dust and dirt that fouls terminations and hampers future maintenance
Lubricant dissolves solid black-iron conduit within 24 hours
explanation: While pulling lubricant reduces friction inside long conduits, any residue left on exposed service loops attracts dust and grime that contaminates connectors and makes future servicing messy.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, pp. 137-138

topic: Multimode versus Single-Mode Fiber Distance Limits
prompt: According to Chapter 6 of the CTS-I Exam Guide, what are the typical maximum transmission distances for audiovisual data over Multimode optical fiber versus Single-Mode optical fiber?
choices: Multimode: 5 m; Single-mode: 100 m
Multimode: 200 km; Single-mode: 2 km
Multimode: 50 m; Single-mode: 500 m
Multimode (bandwidth-limited by modal dispersion): ~2 km (6,560 ft); Single-mode (loss-limited): ~200 km (124 mi)
explanation: Multimode fiber has a wider core where multiple light paths cause modal dispersion (bandwidth-limited to ~2 km / 6,560 ft), whereas single-mode fiber carries a single straight path (loss-limited up to ~200 km / 124 mi).
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, pp. 117-119, 150

topic: Hybrid versus Composite Optical Fiber Cable Construction
prompt: When pulling specialized fiber trunk cables for broadcast cameras or campus racks, what distinguishes a 'Hybrid' fiber cable from a 'Composite' fiber cable?
choices: A Hybrid cable combines optical fibers and copper power conductors under one jacket (e.g., for HD cameras), whereas a Composite cable combines both single-mode and multimode optical fibers under one jacket
A Hybrid cable uses plastic fiber, whereas a Composite cable uses hollow air tubes
A Hybrid cable is for underwater use only, whereas a Composite cable is for aerial poles only
There is no difference; both terms describe standard Cat 5e UTP
explanation: In AV/broadcast cabling, a hybrid cable bundles optical fibers together with copper electrical power conductors, while a composite cable bundles both single-mode and multimode fibers inside one sheath.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, pp. 118-119

topic: Leaving Spare Pull String Inside Populated Conduit
prompt: Whenever an installer finishes pulling a cable bundle through a conduit run, what item should be pulled in alongside the bundle and tied off at both ends?
choices: A live 120 V extension cord
A fresh spare pull string (jet line) secured at both pull boxes for future cable additions
A steel tape measure left permanently inside the pipe
An unshielded consumer RCA patch cable
explanation: Pulling a fresh spare pull string in alongside the cable bundle and tying it off at each junction box allows future cables to be added without having to re-fish the conduit.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, pp. 133-138

topic: Drilling Finished Wood Surfaces Without Exit Splintering
prompt: When drilling a through-hole in a finished wood lectern or architectural panel during rough-in, how should the installer drill to prevent ugly splintering on the visible side?
choices: Use a concrete masonry hammer drill at maximum speed from the back side
Punch the hole through with a claw hammer
Drill from the finished side toward the unfinished back side (or, if finished on both sides, drill a small starter pilot hole through and enlarge from both sides)
Heat the drill bit red-hot with a blowtorch to burn through the wood
explanation: Drill bits splinter wood as they exit the back of a workpiece; always drill from the finished face toward the hidden back, or drill a small pilot hole and bore inward from both faces if both sides are visible.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 7, pp. 170-172

topic: Awl Center-Punch Dimple Before Drilling Hard Metal
prompt: Before drilling a pilot hole into a hard steel plate or metal enclosure during substructure rough-in, what should the installer do so the rotating drill bit does not skate across the surface?
choices: Coat the steel surface with heavy grease
Run the drill backward in hammer mode
Hold the drill bit at a 45-degree angle with one hand
Use a sharp awl or center punch and a hammer to indent a small dimple at the exact pencil mark
explanation: Punching a small dimple into hard metal with an awl/center punch and hammer seats the tip of the HSS drill bit so it starts straight without skating off the mark.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 7, pp. 170-171

topic: Cat 6 versus Cat 6A 10 Gbps Distance Limits
prompt: When pulling twisted-pair infrastructure cable for 10 Gbps AV-over-IP (such as SDVoE), what is the maximum supported 10 Gbps link distance for Category 6 (250 MHz) compared to Category 6A (500 MHz)?
choices: Cat 6 supports 10 Gbps up to 55 m (180 ft), whereas Cat 6A (with internal pair separator reducing alien crosstalk) supports 10 Gbps up to the full 100 m (328 ft)
Cat 6 supports 10 Gbps up to 500 m, whereas Cat 6A is limited to 15 m
Both Cat 6 and Cat 6A are limited to 5 m (16 ft) at 10 Gbps
Neither Cat 6 nor Cat 6A can carry more than 100 Mbps
explanation: Category 6 (250 MHz) is limited to 55 m (180 ft) at 10 Gbps due to alien crosstalk, whereas Category 6A (500 MHz, with a physical spline/separator) supports 10 Gbps over the full 100 m (328 ft) channel.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, pp. 114-116

topic: Category 7 and 7A Non-Recognition by TIA/EIA
prompt: Which statement accurately describes Category 7 (600 MHz) and Category 7A (1 GHz) shielded twisted-pair cables?
choices: They are unshielded 2-pair telephone cables

They are optical fiber cables with yellow jackets

topic: AVIXA F502.02 Unfixed Rack Weight Distribution Rule

topic: RF Receiver and Antenna Placement in Metal Racks

topic: Adjacent Opposite-Airflow Equipment Thermal Loop

Opposite fan directions cancel out the rack's Wi-Fi signal
Side-to-side fans increase the weight of the rack by 50%
It reverses the polarity of balanced XLR audio cables

topic: Isolating Rack Technical Ground from Building Conduit Steel

topic: IEC Class II Double-Insulated Equipment Symbol and Grounding Rule

topic: Rack Thermal Heat Load Calculation in Btu/hr

topic: AVIXA F502.01 Opposite-Side Signal Separation and 100 mm Spacing

topic: Detachable versus Captive Power Cord Bundling in Racks

topic: Hook-and-Loop Ties versus Tight Nylon Zip-Ties on Rack Bundles

topic: Balanced Differential Circuit Common-Mode Rejection (CMRR)

topic: Digital Video Cliff Effect and Passive HDMI Barrel Couplers

topic: Motorized Screen Roller Wrap Limit Switch Adjustment

topic: Optical Rear-Projection Screen Orientation (Fresnel vs. Lenticular)

topic: Equal Parallel Loudspeaker Impedance Calculation

topic: Wireless Diversity Antenna Spacing and Metal Clearance

topic: Coaxial BNC Cable Stripping and Linear Compression Termination Sequence

topic: AVIXA F501.01 Permanent Cable Label Placement Distance

topic: Insulation Displacement (IDC) Solid versus Stranded 8P8C Contacts

topic: T568A versus T568B Pinout and Crossover Cables

topic: Lead-Free Solder Melting Temperature Difference

topic: Optical Fiber Termination Safety (Black Mat and Laser Eye Safety)

topic: Ruggedized Field Fiber Connectors (Expanded Beam and opticalCON)

topic: Audio System Power-On and Power-Off Sequencing

topic: OSI Model Layer 2 (Data Link) versus Layer 3 (Network) Addressing

Layer 2 (Data Link layer) uses MAC addresses for local switch forwarding, and Layer 3 (Network layer) uses IP addresses for routing across networks
Layer 6 uses MAC addresses; Layer 5 uses IP addresses

source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 12, pp. 288-293

topic: Layer 2 (AVB) versus Layer 3 (Dante, AES67, ST 2110) Networked AV Protocols

topic: Reserve DHCP Best Practice for AV Endpoints
prompt: Why does AVIXA recommend using 'Reserve DHCP' rather than manual static IP entry or standard dynamic DHCP leases when configuring IP addresses on enterprise AV equipment?

Reserve DHCP encrypts HDMI cables against HDCP locality checks
Reserve DHCP eliminates the need for network switches or patch cables

topic: Diagnosing APIPA 169.254.x.x Link-Local Address on ipconfig

topic: IPv4 CIDR /18 Subnet Mask and Splitting Subnets

256 subnets

source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 12, pp. 297-298

topic: TCP versus UDP Transport Layer Selection for AV Control and Media

topic: EDID Handshake Sequence Between Source and Sink

topic: 50% Enterprise Network Bandwidth Rule and 20-Device SPOF Limit

topic: Using ping and arp -a to Remotely Discover a Device MAC Address

topic: IPv6 128-Bit Address Structure and Double-Colon Compression

topic: QoS DiffServ Multimedia Conferencing versus Real-Time Interactive Classes

topic: VLAN 802.1Q Broadcast Domain Isolation and Inter-VLAN Routing

topic: Control Function versus Macro Distinction

RS-232, RS-422, and RS-485 are wireless RF protocols operating at 2.4 GHz

topic: Momentary versus Latching Contact Closure Control

topic: Infrared (IR) Control Limitations and Three Field Tricks

topic: Camera Zoom Focus and Mechanical Back-Focus Alignment Sequence

topic: Zigbee versus Bluetooth versus Ultra-Wideband (UWB) RF Control

topic: Disabling Both Hardware and Software AEC Double-Processing

topic: Gated versus Gain-Sharing Automatic Microphone Mixers

choices: Both are designed exclusively for mixing live rock bands and symphony orchestras
Gated mixers adjust projector brightness, while gain-sharing mixers adjust screen height

Used strictly for speech applications (never music), a gated automixer switches mic channels on or off across a threshold, whereas a gain-sharing automixer continuously rides all channel gains so total system gain remains constant
Gain-sharing mixers apply +48V phantom power only when a talker whispers
explanation: Automatic mixers are used strictly for speech (panel discussions, boardrooms); gated automixers open/close channels at a threshold, while gain-sharing automixers continuously distribute a constant total gain pool across all mics.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 9, pp. 215-216

topic: EDID Emulator Configuration for Mixed-Resolution Displays
prompt: A presentation switcher output feeds both a 4K UHD (3840 × 2160) main wall display and a 1080p (1920 × 1080) confidence monitor via a non-scaling distribution amplifier. How should the EDID emulator/manager be configured?
choices: Set the EDID to 8K (7680 × 4320) so neither display works
Disconnect the Display Data Channel (DDC) pin 19 completely
Set the EDID to 4:3 (640 × 480) interlaced
Configure the EDID manager to present the highest common native resolution and aspect ratio supported by all connected displays (in this case, 1080p at 16:9)
explanation: When one unscaled source feeds multiple displays with different native resolutions, the EDID manager should advertise the highest common resolution (and shared 16:9 aspect ratio) supported by every connected sink.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 15, pp. 355-356

topic: Projector Eco/Standby Mode Disabling LAN and RS-232 Ports
prompt: During control system testing, a ceiling projector responds to every RS-232 and IP command while powered on, but refuses to turn back on after being shut down by the touch panel. Which device menu setting is the most likely culprit?
choices: The projector's 'Eco / Low-Power Standby' menu mode is enabled, which shuts down power to its LAN and RS-232 control receiver boards when the projector enters standby
The projector's optical zoom lens is set to the center 2/3 of its range
The screen gain is 1.0 matte white
The touch panel is using TCP instead of UDP
explanation: Many displays and projectors default to an energy-saving 'Eco Standby' mode that turns off the internal RS-232/LAN communication board when powered down; set standby mode to 'Normal / Network Standby On' so wake-up commands are received.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 13, pp. 319-320

topic: Capacitive Reactance (XC) High-Frequency Attenuation in Long Cables
prompt: As the frequency of an alternating current (AC) or digital signal increases (`f ↑`), how does Capacitive Reactance (`XC`) behave between parallel cable conductors, and what effect does this have on long cable runs?
choices: XC increases with frequency, boosting high treble frequencies by +12 dB

XC decreases as frequency increases (`f ↑ ⇒ XC ↓`), allowing high-frequency signal energy to shunt across the dielectric capacitance between conductors—causing high-frequency roll-off and rounding digital pulses
XC remains constant at 75 ohms at all frequencies from 0 Hz to 10 GHz
XC converts AC signals into continuous DC battery power
explanation: Capacitive reactance (XC) is inversely proportional to frequency; as frequency rises, XC drops, shunting high frequencies between parallel conductors and causing high-frequency loss over long cables.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 11, pp. 269-271

topic: Inductive Reactance (XL) and Magnetic Crosstalk
prompt: Unlike capacitive reactance, how does Inductive Reactance (`XL`) change as frequency increases (`f ↑`), and how does magnetic induction affect adjacent unshielded cables?
choices: XL drops to zero at high frequencies
XL only exists in optical glass fibers
XL increases as frequency increases (`f ↑ ⇒ XL ↑`), and alternating magnetic fields around current-carrying conductors induce unwanted voltage (hum or crosstalk) into adjacent parallel conductors
XL eliminates the need for twisted-pair cabling
explanation: Inductive reactance (XL) increases with frequency, opposing rapid current changes, while expanding/collapsing magnetic fields around AC power or signal wires induce crosstalk and 50/60 Hz hum into nearby conductors.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 11, pp. 270-272

topic: Safety Earth / Protective Ground Rules (First-Make, Last-Break)
prompt: Which statement correctly states the mandatory electrical safety rules for the AC mains Safety Earth / Protective Ground conductor in an AV installation?
choices: A 10-amp fuse and toggle switch must be installed inline on every green/yellow safety earth wire
Using a 3-prong-to-2-prong 'ground lifter' cheater plug is the AVIXA-approved method to eliminate audio hum
The safety earth pin on a power connector must be shorter than the Live and Neutral pins so it disconnects first

The safety earth path must be continuous and unswitched (never containing a switch, fuse, or breaker), its connector pin must be 'first-make, last-break', and it must never be lifted to fix a ground loop
explanation: Safety earth/ground protects human life from chassis faults; it must never contain a switch, fuse, or breaker, must make contact first and break contact last on plugs, and must never be defeated with a ground lifter.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 11, pp. 275-277

topic: 22 AWG Copper Wire DC Resistance per 30 m (100 ft)
prompt: When performing an unpowered DC resistance/continuity check on a 30 m (100 ft) run of 22 AWG copper wire with a zeroed digital multimeter, approximately what resistance reading should the installer expect on each conductor?
choices: Approximately 2 Ω per 30 m (100 ft), or ~17 Ω per 300 m (1,000 ft)
Approximately 10,000 Ω per 30 m
Exactly 0.000 Ω regardless of length
Approximately 75 Ω at DC
explanation: Standard 22 AWG copper conductor exhibits ~17 Ω of DC resistance per 300 m (1,000 ft), which equates to ~1.7 to 2 Ω per 30 m (100 ft) one-way (~3.5–4 Ω loop resistance with the far end shorted).
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, pp. 145-146

topic: Unequal Parallel Loudspeaker Impedance Calculation (4, 8, and 16 Ohms)
prompt: During pre-connection verification, an installer checks a parallel circuit combining one 4-ohm loudspeaker, one 8-ohm loudspeaker, and one 16-ohm loudspeaker. What is the total calculated impedance (`ZT`) of this parallel combination?
explanation: Using ZT = 1 ÷ (1/Z1 + 1/Z2 + 1/Z3): 1 ÷ (0.25 + 0.125 + 0.0625) = 1 ÷ 0.4375 = 2.29 Ω. Notice that parallel impedance is always smaller than the lowest individual speaker impedance (4 Ω).
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 9, pp. 224-225, 229

topic: Series-Parallel Loudspeaker Impedance Calculation (Two Branches of Three 8-Ohm Speakers)
prompt: Six 8-ohm loudspeakers are wired in a series-parallel array consisting of two parallel branches, where each branch contains three 8-ohm loudspeakers wired in series. What is the total load impedance (`ZT`) presented to the amplifier?
choices: 12 Ω (each series branch is `8 + 8 + 8 = 24 Ω`, and two 24 Ω branches in parallel equal `24 ÷ 2 = 12 Ω`)
8 Ω
explanation: First sum the series speakers in each branch (8 + 8 + 8 = 24 Ω per branch), then combine the two equal 24 Ω branches in parallel (24 Ω ÷ 2 = 12 Ω).
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 9, p. 225

topic: Interpreting High versus Low Impedance Meter Readings on Speaker Lines
prompt: When testing a disconnected 70V loudspeaker line with an AC impedance meter (`Z`-meter), why is a reading much LOWER than calculated far more dangerous to the amplifier than a reading much HIGHER than calculated?
choices: A low impedance reading means all speakers are unplugged and safe
A high impedance reading will instantly melt the amplifier's output transistors
Impedance meters only measure optical fiber loss

A reading much lower than expected indicates a short circuit, a backward-wired step-down transformer, or an direct 8-ohm speaker on a 70V line—which will draw excessive current and destroy the amplifier output stage
explanation: By Ohm's law (I = V/Z), a much lower impedance than expected draws dangerously high current that overloads and burns out the amplifier, whereas a higher reading indicates an open branch or under-tapped transformer.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 9, pp. 226-227

topic: HDCP 2.x Repeater Cascade Limits (32 Devices and 4 Levels) and Locality Check
prompt: When verifying High-Bandwidth Digital Content Protection (HDCP 2.x) across a matrix switcher and extender chain, what are the maximum supported device count, maximum repeater cascade depth, and locality-check round-trip time limit?
choices: Up to 32 connected devices maximum, up to 4 repeater levels deep, and a locality check round-trip of < 20 ms (7 ms timer per attempt)
Up to 1,024 connected devices, 16 repeater levels, and a 5-second locality timer
Up to 2 devices total, 0 repeaters allowed, and native support over coaxial SDI
Unlimited devices and repeaters as long as passive baluns are used
explanation: HDCP 2.x supports a maximum of 32 connected devices across up to 4 cascaded repeater levels, with an initial key return ≤ 100 ms and a locality check requiring round-trip response in < 20 ms (7 ms timer).
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 15, pp. 356-358

topic: SDI Lack of HDCP Encryption Support
prompt: A technician converts an HDMI output from a Blu-ray player or MacBook into 3G-SDI to run 80 m over existing 75-ohm coax to a projector. Why does the projector display a blank or green screen when protected content is played?
choices: 3G-SDI only carries analog audio
SMPTE SDI interfaces do NOT support HDCP encryption; whenever a source requires HDCP authentication (including many Apple devices and Blu-ray players), converting to SDI breaks the HDCP handshake
75-ohm BNC connectors block progressive scan frames
The coax cable needs +48V phantom power
explanation: SDI is an unencrypted professional broadcast interface that has no mechanism for HDCP key exchange; HDCP-encrypted sources will refuse to pass video through an HDMI-to-SDI converter.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 10, p. 237; Chapter 15, pp. 356-357

topic: ANSI/AVIXA V201.01 (ISCR) Four Viewing Categories and Contrast Ratios
prompt: Under the ANSI/AVIXA V201.01 (and 3M-2011) Image System Contrast Ratio standard, what are the minimum required contrast ratios for the four viewing categories?
choices: Passive: 1:1; BDM: 2:1; ADM: 5:1; Full-Motion Video: 10:1
Passive: 100:1; BDM: 50:1; ADM: 15:1; Full-Motion Video: 7:1
Passive Viewing: 7:1; Basic Decision-Making (BDM, e.g., classrooms/boardrooms): 15:1; Analytical Decision-Making (ADM, e.g., medical/CAD): 50:1; Full-Motion Video (FMV): 80:1
All four categories require a minimum 1,000:1 contrast ratio
explanation: ISCR defines four minimum contrast ratios measured under normal room ambient light: 7:1 for Passive Viewing, 15:1 for Basic Decision-Making (BDM), 50:1 for Analytical Decision-Making (ADM), and 80:1 for Full-Motion Video (FMV).
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 15, pp. 363-365

topic: ISCR 5-Location, 16-Zone Checkerboard Measurement Procedure
prompt: When performing an ANSI/AVIXA V201.01 ISCR contrast verification test in a conference room, what test pattern is displayed and how many viewer locations and checkerboard rectangles are measured with a spot luminance meter?
choices: A solid red screen measured from 1 location behind the screen
SMPTE color bars measured with an incident lux meter pressed against the projector lens
A 4-square pattern measured with the room lights turned completely off

A 16-zone black-and-white checkerboard pattern (8 white and 8 black rectangles) measured under normal ambient room light from 5 viewer locations (Front-Left, Front-Right, Center, Rear-Left, Rear-Right)
explanation: ISCR verification projects a 16-zone checkerboard pattern under normal ambient lighting and measures the luminance of all 8 white and 8 black squares from 5 defined viewer locations (CR = Avg White ÷ Avg Black).
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 15, pp. 364-366

topic: ISCR Contrast Ratio Calculation and Conformance Grading
prompt: At Viewer Location 3 in a university lecture hall (Basic Decision-Making category, minimum 15:1), the average luminance of the 8 white checkerboard squares is 240 nits (`cd/m²`) and the average of the 8 black squares is 12 nits. What is the contrast ratio at Location 3, and when is a system graded 'Partially Conforms'?
choices: Contrast ratio is 20:1 (240 ÷ 12 = 20:1, which conforms); a system 'Partially Conforms' if 1 to 4 locations fall below the minimum ratio by no more than 10%
Contrast ratio is 2,880:1; a system partially conforms if all 5 locations fail by 50%
Contrast ratio is 12:1; a system conforms if at least 1 location exceeds 7:1
Contrast ratio is 228:1 (240 − 12)
explanation: Contrast Ratio = Average White Luminance ÷ Average Black Luminance = 240 ÷ 12 = 20:1 (exceeding the 15:1 BDM threshold). Under V201.01, 'Partially Conforms' means 1 to 4 locations miss the target by ≤ 10%.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 15, pp. 365-366; Appendix A, p. 430

topic: Audio/Video Lip-Sync Blip-and-Flash Tolerance Window
prompt: When verifying audio/video lip-sync alignment using a 1-frame 'blip-and-flash' test generator (`AVP-103`), what is the standard broadcast/verification sync tolerance window, and which signal usually needs delay added?
choices: Audio may lead video by +500 ms; add video frame delay to slow the projector down

Audio must stay within +15 ms (lead) to −45 ms (lag) for broadcast/verification (+40 ms to −60 ms general max); because video scalers/displays take longer to process frames, DSP delay is added to the audio path
Audio must lag behind video by at least 200 ms
Lip-sync only needs to be checked at the rack headphone jack, never at the seating area or streaming/recording feeds
explanation: Video scaling and display processing introduce much greater latency than audio chains, causing audio to arrive early; DSP audio delay is added so lip-sync stays within +15 ms lead to −45 ms lag at seats, recorders, and streaming codecs.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 15, pp. 366-367

topic: ANSI/AVIXA 10:2013 AVP-105 Actual User Source Verification Rule
prompt: Why does ANSI/INFOCOMM 10:2013 verification item `AVP-105` explicitly prohibit using a dedicated audio/video test pattern generator for the final end-to-end system verification check?
choices: Because test pattern generators consume too much battery power
Because test pattern generators cannot output 1 kHz sine waves

Because AVP-105 requires verifying end-to-end system performance using an actual typical user source (such as the client's laptop, media player, or VTC codec) to prove real-world EDID, HDCP, scaling, and audio routing
Because test generators are banned by the local fire marshal
explanation: While calibrated test generators are used for setup metrics, AVP-105 requires testing with an actual typical user source device to verify that real-world handshakes, aspect ratios, and audio formats pass cleanly.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 15, p. 369

topic: OTDR (Optical Time-Domain Reflectometer) Fiber Testing
prompt: Which Layer 1 optical fiber test instrument injects light pulses into a fiber strand and analyzes back-scattered/reflected light over time to measure total fiber length, splice attenuation, and the exact distance in meters to a cable break?
choices: An inductive tone generator and wand
A 3-lamp AC polarity tester
A Class 2 SPL meter
An Optical Time-Domain Reflectometer (OTDR)
explanation: An Optical Time-Domain Reflectometer (OTDR) measures the timing and amplitude of reflected light pulses to map fiber length, connector/splice losses, and the exact distance to any fracture.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 12, p. 305

topic: NIC Loopback Plug and 127.0.0.1 Local Stack Verification
prompt: During network troubleshooting, what is the difference between pinging the loopback address `127.0.0.1` versus inserting a physical hardware NIC loopback plug into the Ethernet port?
choices: Pinging 127.0.0.1 tests the local TCP/IP software stack, whereas a physical NIC loopback plug wires the transmit (TX) pins back to the receive (RX) pins to prove the physical NIC transceiver hardware works
Pinging 127.0.0.1 tests the remote ISP gateway, whereas a loopback plug tests the ceiling projector lamp
Both tests measure the PoE wattage of the remote network switch
Loopback plugs are used to terminate RS-485 buses with 120 ohms
explanation: Pinging 127.0.0.1 verifies that the computer's internal TCP/IP software stack is functioning, while a physical NIC loopback plug loops TX to RX at the jack to verify the physical Layer 1/2 transceiver hardware.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 12, pp. 298, 305-306

topic: Interpreting a Single Asterisk (*) Timeout in tracert Output
prompt: When running `tracert` (or `traceroute`) to diagnose a path across an enterprise WAN, Hop 4 displays `* * * Request timed out`, but Hops 5, 6, and the final destination AV server reply with normal 12 ms round-trip times. What does the Hop 4 timeout indicate?
choices: The fiber-optic cable between Hop 3 and Hop 4 has been severed completely
The intermediate router at Hop 4 is simply configured to deprioritize or block ICMP echo requests for security, while still forwarding normal IP traffic to the destination
The destination server has an invalid subnet mask
The local laptop's NIC card is burned out
explanation: If `tracert` reaches the final destination successfully, a `*` timeout at an intermediate router simply means that router's firewall/ACL blocks ICMP TTL-expired replies rather than indicating a broken route.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 12, pp. 306-307

topic: SPL Meter Class 1 versus Class 2 Tolerances and A/C/Z Weighting
prompt: Under IEC 61672-1 / ANSI S1.4, what are the accuracy tolerances of Class 1 and Class 2 SPL meters, and when should A-weighting (`dBA`), C-weighting (`dBC`), and Z-weighting (`dBZ`) be selected?
choices: Class 1 is ±5 dB and Class 2 is ±10 dB; A-weighting is for concerts and C-weighting is for quiet HVAC
Class 1 and Class 2 both have ±0.01 dB tolerance; Z-weighting rolls off everything below 1 kHz

Class 1 is ±0.7 dB (precision) and Class 2 is ±1.0 dB (general field); use A-weighting for low levels/ambient noise/speech (20–55 dB), C-weighting for high levels (85–140 dB), and Z-weighting for flat 10 Hz–20 kHz response
SPL meters measure electrical voltage in dBu rather than acoustic pressure
explanation: Class 1 (±0.7 dB) and Class 2 (±1.0 dB) SPL meters use A-weighting to match human low-level ear roll-off for HVAC/speech, C-weighting for high-SPL program levels, and Z-weighting (Zero) for an unweighted flat response.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 14, pp. 325-327

topic: Neutralizing Dynamic Processors Before Setting Gain Structure
prompt: Before injecting a test tone to set Unity Gain or System Optimization across an audio signal chain, how must equalizers, compressors/limiters, and downward expanders/gates be configured?
choices: Set all EQ bands to +12 dB boost, compressor thresholds to minimum, and gate thresholds to maximum
Leave all effects and dynamics active so they compress the 1 kHz sine wave
Turn power amplifiers ON to maximum before touching the mixer
Turn power amplifiers OFF, set all EQ filters to 0 dB (flat), set compressor and limiter thresholds to MAXIMUM, set expander and gate thresholds to MINIMUM, and turn off effects
explanation: To prevent dynamics processors from altering test-tone levels during gain staging, set compressor/limiter thresholds to maximum (so they do not compress), expander/gate thresholds to minimum (so they do not gate), and EQs flat—with power amps OFF.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 14, pp. 330-331

topic: Unity Gain (1 kHz + DMM) versus System Optimization (400 Hz + Piezo)
prompt: Why does the Unity Gain method use a `1 kHz` sine wave and a True RMS Multimeter (targeting `0.775 V` [`0 dBu`] or `1.23 V` [`+4 dBu`] at each stage), whereas System Optimization uses a `400 Hz` sine wave and a piezo tweeter?
choices: Unity Gain sets identical input/output voltage across all stages for standard rooms (~60 dB S/N), whereas System Optimization uses a 400 Hz tone below the piezo's 2–20 kHz passband so the piezo stays silent until clipping harmonics (> 2 kHz) make it buzz—maximizing S/N and relative headroom for critical halls
A 1 kHz tone destroys piezo tweeters, whereas a 400 Hz tone cannot be read by a multimeter
Unity Gain is used only on 70V speaker lines, whereas System Optimization is used only on optical fiber
Both methods require the power amplifiers to be turned full up during step 1
explanation: Unity Gain matches nominal voltages (0.775 V or 1.23 V at 1 kHz) for fast, swappable setup in conference rooms, while System Optimization drives a 400 Hz tone until clipping harmonics (> 2 kHz) buzz a piezo tweeter, aligning clip points across all stages for maximum S/N.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 14, pp. 329-334

topic: Microphone Preamp Calibration and NOM −3 dB Doubling Rule
prompt: After calibrating a conference room's four tabletop microphones individually with `65–70 dB SPL` pink noise at the capsule so each reaches `0` on the mixer meter, how much should each mic's input trim be reduced if all four microphones will remain open simultaneously (`NOM = 4`)?
choices: Boost each microphone trim by +6 dB
Reduce each microphone trim by −6 dB (−3 dB for every doubling of simultaneously open microphones: 1 → 2 = −3 dB; 2 → 4 = −6 dB)
Reduce each microphone trim by −40 dB
Leave all four trims at +20 dB and turn off the power amplifier
explanation: Every doubling of simultaneously active microphones (NOM) adds 3 dB of summed acoustic/electronic energy (`10 log(NOM)`); for 4 open mics (two doublings: 1→2→4), reduce each mic preamp trim by 6 dB.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 14, pp. 334-336; Appendix A, p. 431

topic: Power Amplifier Input Attenuator Calibration and Hiss Prevention
prompt: What is the true function of the front-panel rotary knobs on a power amplifier, and what symptom occurs if an installer leaves them wide open ('all the way up') while turning the upstream DSP/mixer outputs way down?
choices: They adjust the amplifier's AC mains power consumption; turning them up saves electricity
They adjust the loudspeaker's physical impedance from 4 ohms to 70 volts

They are input attenuators (not wattage controls) that must be set LAST by raising them from minimum just until target room SPL is reached; leaving them wide open amplifies upstream noise floors and causes constant audible system hiss
They control the room's reverberation time (RT60)
explanation: Power amplifier level controls are input attenuators; setting them wide open while starving the upstream mixer/DSP output degrades signal-to-noise ratio and produces constant loudspeaker hiss when idle.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 14, pp. 336-337

topic: Simplified Room Mode Floor Formula (f_mode = 3v / RSD)
prompt: Before equalizing a conference room that measures 9.0 m long, 6.0 m wide, and 3.43 m high (`v = 343 m/s`), the installer calculates the simplified room mode frequency (`f_mode = [3 × v] ÷ RSD`). Below what frequency do standing-wave room modes dominate (where RTA equalization must NOT be attempted)?
choices: 300 Hz (`[3 × 343 m/s] ÷ 3.43 m smallest dimension = 300 Hz`)
explanation: Using the room's smallest dimension (RSD = 3.43 m ceiling height), f_mode = (3 × 343 m/s) ÷ 3.43 m = 300 Hz. Standing-wave room modes below this frequency cannot be fixed with an RTA/EQ.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 14, pp. 338-339; Appendix A, p. 431

topic: RTA Measurement Microphone Placement (Critical Distance Dc + 3 dB)
prompt: Because a single-channel Real-Time Analyzer (RTA) is 'time-blind' and cannot distinguish direct loudspeaker sound from room reflections, how do you locate the proper measurement microphone position?
choices: Inject pink noise 20 dB above ambient, walk the omnidirectional mic away from the speaker until SPL stops dropping (Critical Distance Dc), then move closer toward the speaker until SPL rises by +3 dB (staying ≥ 1 m / 3 ft from the cabinet)
Press the measurement microphone directly against the tweeter grille at 0 mm
Place the microphone inside the hallway outside the room with the door closed
Hang a figure-8 ribbon microphone 10 cm below the HVAC supply diffuser
explanation: Walking away from the speaker until SPL plateaus identifies Critical Distance (Dc, where direct sound equals reverberant sound); stepping back toward the speaker until SPL rises +3 dB places the mic inside the direct field (while staying ≥ 1 m away).
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 14, pp. 339-341

topic: RTA Cut-Only Equalization Rule and 6 dB Maximum Cut Limit
prompt: When equalizing a loudspeaker system with an RTA, why should the installer use the 'cut-only' method and never exceed `6 dB` of attenuation on any filter band?
choices: Boosting EQ bands reduces amplifier power consumption

Boosting peaks eats up amplifier headroom and increases distortion, while any response dip or peak requiring more than 6 dB of correction (or showing no change on the RTA) is an acoustic phase/comb cancellation that cannot be fixed with EQ
Equalizers are physically incapable of cutting more than 2 dB
Cutting more than 6 dB reverses the polarity of the subwoofer
explanation: Equalization should cut peaks (≤ 6 dB max) rather than boost dips; any anomaly needing > 6 dB or failing to respond on the analyzer is a non-minimum-phase acoustic cancellation that boosting would only drive into clipping.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 14, pp. 341-342

topic: Dual-Channel FFT Time Windowing and Comb Filter Interpretation (5–30 ms)
prompt: When using a Dual-Channel FFT analyzer with the mic in the far field (`3× to 10×` source size), an early reflection arriving between `5 ms and 30 ms` after direct sound causes comb filtering. How should the technician interpret the comb-filtered trace?
choices: Apply +20 dB narrow parametric boosts to fill in every deep cancellation notch
Turn off time windowing so the analyzer averages 10 seconds of room echo

Ignore the deep destructive cancellation notches (which shift frequency if the mic moves 50 mm) and read the true loudspeaker response as 3 to 6 dB below the constructive peaks—or place the mic on a boundary surface to minimize the reflection
Replace the Dual-Channel FFT with a simple continuity buzzer
explanation: In a 5–30 ms comb filter, constructive peaks add at most +3 to +6 dB while destructive notches plunge 20–40 dB deep; always ignore the notches and read the true response 3–6 dB below the peaks.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 14, pp. 342-347

topic: Subwoofer Near-Field Port-Summing Equalization Technique
prompt: To measure and equalize a vented subwoofer below the room-mode frequency floor using Dual-Channel FFT, Mic 1 is placed at the woofer dust cap and Mic 2 is placed in the cabinet port. If the port area is `1/2` of the woofer's moving-piston area, how is the port mic scaled before summing?
choices: Boost the port mic by +10 dB
Mute the woofer dust-cap mic completely
Invert the polarity of the port mic and add 50 ms of delay
Attenuate the port microphone by −3 dB (or by −6 dB if the port area is 1/4 of the piston area) before power-summing the two curves
explanation: In near-field subwoofer port summing, the port mic level is scaled by the ratio of port area to woofer piston area: −3 dB when port area is 1/2 of piston area, and −6 dB when port area is 1/4 of piston area.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 14, pp. 347-348

topic: Camera White Balance Procedure with Matte White Reference Card
prompt: What is the proper field procedure for setting accurate White Balance on a PTZ or broadcast camera in a lecture hall?
choices: Place a matte white card at the presenter's actual position illuminated by the normal room/stage lighting, zoom the camera in until the white card fills the frame, and trigger White Balance
Aim the camera directly into a bare ceiling LED fixture and press White Balance
Turn off all room lights, cap the lens, and press White Balance
Hold a glossy mirror in front of the lens under sunlight in the parking lot
explanation: White balance must be calibrated under the exact Kelvin color temperature illuminating the subject by filling the zoomed-in frame with a non-reflective matte white card held at the subject's position.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 15, pp. 361-362

topic: Camera Lighting Defects (White Holes, AGC Sparkles, and Backlight Compensation)
prompt: During camera setup, a presenter standing in front of an uncovered exterior window looks dark, and enabling the camera's 'Backlight' or 'AGC' setting causes blown-out 'white holes' or grainy 'sparkles.' What is the proper permanent remedy?
choices: Set the electronic shutter speed to 1/10,000 second to create stroboscopic motion
Control the room lighting instead of relying on electronic camera compensation: close window shades/apply ND film to reduce background contrast and add high-CRI front illumination on the presenter
Turn chroma saturation to 100% and defocus the lens
Mount the camera upside down without flipping the image
explanation: 'White holes' occur when scene contrast exceeds sensor dynamic range, and 'sparkles' occur when low light forces AGC to boost electronic noise; fix the physical lighting/window contrast rather than using Backlight or AGC.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 10, pp. 239-240; Chapter 15, pp. 360-361

topic: Display Calibration Sequence Using PLUGE and SMPTE/ARIB Color Bars
prompt: When calibrating a display or projector's picture controls, which adjustments must be completed FIRST using a monochrome PLUGE / grayscale pattern before adjusting Chroma and Hue with color bars?
choices: Adjust Hue first using a solid blue screen, then set Keystone
Set Sharpness to 100% before turning the display on

Calibrate Contrast (white level) using the Super White (Step 255) bar until just below white clipping, and Brightness (black level) using Normal Black (Step 16) vs. Super Black (Step 0) PLUGE bars until barely indistinguishable—before adjusting Chroma/Hue
Adjust audio delay first to fix black level
explanation: Monochrome dynamic range must be calibrated before color: set Contrast using the Step 255 Super White bar and Brightness using the Step 16 Black / Step 0 Super Black PLUGE bars, then set Chroma and Hue with SMPTE/ARIB color bars.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 15, pp. 362-363

topic: Projector Mechanical Alignment and Optical Lens Shift versus Electronic Keystone
prompt: Why must an installer complete all mechanical projector positioning (`x/y/z`, roll/pitch/yaw) and use Optical Keystone Correction (Lens Shift) rather than Electronic Keystone Correction?
choices: Electronic keystone causes the projector lamp to explode
Optical lens shift reduces the projector's lumen output by 90%
Mechanical alignment only works on CRT projectors
Electronic keystone digitally rescales and compresses scan lines to counter the trapezoid, permanently discarding native pixel resolution and fine image detail
explanation: Mechanical alignment and optical lens shift move the optical image without losing a single pixel, whereas electronic keystone correction compresses scan lines onto fewer pixels and degrades image detail.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 10, pp. 255-258

topic: Projector Zoom Range Center Two-Thirds Sweet Spot
prompt: When positioning a ceiling projector and adjusting its zoom lens to fill the screen border, why should the installer target the center two-thirds (`2/3`) of the lens zoom range rather than the extreme wide or telephoto limit?
choices: Optical aberrations (such as curvature of field, spherical aberration, and dispersion) are minimized in the center two-thirds of the zoom range, and it leaves room for the manufacturer's 3%–5% throw tolerance
Using the center of the zoom range doubles the refresh rate from 60 Hz to 120 Hz
Extreme telephoto zoom disables the HDMI input
Zoom lenses cannot focus anywhere outside the exact midpoint
explanation: Primary optical aberrations peak at the extreme ends of a zoom lens (especially curvature of field at wide angle); designing and mounting for the center 2/3 of the zoom range maximizes sharpness and absorbs 3%–5% throw tolerances.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 10, pp. 243-244, 255

topic: Decibel Distance Inverse Square Law Calculation (−6 dB per Doubling)
prompt: During audio coverage verification in an auditorium, an SPL meter reads `82 dB SPL` at a seat located `4 m` from the loudspeaker. Assuming free-field inverse-square propagation (`ΔdB = 20 log(D1/D2)`), what SPL will be measured at a seat `16 m` from the loudspeaker?
choices: 79 dB SPL (−3 dB)
70 dB SPL (−12 dB across two doublings of distance: 4 m → 8 m → 16 m)
76 dB SPL (−6 dB)
62 dB SPL (−20 dB)
explanation: Moving from 4 m to 16 m represents two doublings of distance (4 → 8 → 16 m). By the inverse-square law, ΔdB = 20 log(4/16) = −12.04 dB, dropping the level from 82 dB SPL to 70 dB SPL.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 9, pp. 206-207; Appendix A, p. 431

topic: Decibel Power Ratio Calculation (10 log P1/P2 and +10 dB Twice as Loud)
prompt: If a 100 W power amplifier is replaced with a 400 W power amplifier driving the same loudspeaker load (`ΔdB = 10 log(P1/P2)`), how many decibels of additional output headroom are gained, and what power increase is required to sound 'twice as loud' (`+10 dB`)?
choices: +12 dB from 400 W; 2× power sounds twice as loud
+3 dB from 400 W; 4× power sounds twice as loud
+6 dB from 400 W (two doublings of power: 100 → 200 → 400 W); a 10× power increase (1,000 W) is required for a +10 dB change perceived as 'twice as loud'
+40 dB from 400 W
explanation: Using ΔdB = 10 log(400/100) = +6 dB (each doubling of power adds +3 dB). To achieve a +10 dB increase—which human hearing perceives as twice as loud—requires 10 times the amplifier wattage.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 9, pp. 205-207; Appendix A, p. 431

topic: Electronic Delay Calculation for Under-Balcony Fill Loudspeakers
prompt: In a large auditorium where sound travels in air at `343 m/s` (`1,125 ft/s`), an under-balcony delay loudspeaker is mounted `17.15 m` downrange from the main stage array. Approximately how many milliseconds of electronic delay must be set in the DSP so the main and fill arrivals align?
choices: 5 ms
500 ms
50 ms (`17.15 m ÷ 343 m/s = 0.050 s = 50 ms`, plus a small Haas precedence offset if specified)
explanation: Because electrical signals travel near the speed of light while acoustic waves travel at 343 m/s (~2.9 ms per meter), a speaker 17.15 m downrange requires 17.15 ÷ 343 = 0.050 s (50 ms) of DSP delay.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 9, pp. 218-219

topic: Loudspeaker Crossover Filter Order Slope (6 dB per Octave per Order)
prompt: When configuring a high-pass or crossover filter in an audio DSP, at what rate in decibels per octave does filter attenuation increase for each filter order (`1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th order`)?
choices: 6 dB per octave per filter order (1st order = 6 dB/octave, 2nd order = 12 dB/octave, 3rd order = 18 dB/octave, 4th order = 24 dB/octave)
1 dB per octave per filter order
20 dB per octave per filter order
Filter order only affects phase, never attenuation slope
explanation: Every filter order adds 6 dB per octave of roll-off slope: a 1st-order filter rolls off at 6 dB/octave, a 2nd-order at 12 dB/octave, a 3rd-order at 18 dB/octave, and a 4th-order at 24 dB/octave.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 9, p. 218

topic: Microphone Polar Pattern Placement Relative to Loudspeakers
prompt: When aiming a cardioid or hypercardioid lectern microphone in a room with overhead loudspeakers, where are the microphone's maximum rejection nulls located to maximize gain before feedback?
choices: Directly on-axis (0 degrees) at the front of the capsule

Cardioid has maximum rejection directly at the rear (180°), whereas hypercardioid and supercardioid have tighter side pickup with small rear lobes—so maximum rejection nulls sit off-axis toward the rear cones (~110°–125°)
Omnidirectional microphones have a 40 dB null at 90 degrees
Bidirectional (figure-8) microphones reject sound equally from the front and back
explanation: A pure cardioid rejects sound at 180° (directly behind), while hypercardioid and supercardioid patterns trade a small 180° rear lobe for deeper off-axis rejection cones; aim the null (not the rear lobe) toward loudspeakers.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 9, pp. 210-212

topic: Loudspeaker Polarity Verification (`AP-108` Pulse Tester and Battery Test)
prompt: Why must loudspeaker polarity (`AP-108`) be verified across all installed cabinets in a room, and how do an electronic polarity pulse tester or a momentary low-voltage battery touch confirm positive polarity?
choices: Reversed polarity causes the loudspeaker transformer to catch fire
Polarity only matters for constant-voltage 100V horns, never for low-frequency woofers

An out-of-phase speaker cancels low-frequency bass energy from adjacent speakers; an acoustic polarity pulse detector reads '+' (or touching battery '+' to speaker '+' pushes the woofer cone outward/forward)
Positive polarity pulls the woofer cone inward toward the magnet
explanation: When one speaker in a pair is wired with reversed polarity, their low frequencies cancel acoustically; polarity pulse testers verify acoustic phase (`AP-108`), and positive DC voltage pushes a woofer cone outward.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 11, p. 268; Chapter 14, p. 350

topic: Assistive Listening System (ALS) Induction Loop and T-Coil Verification (`AP-113`)
prompt: When installing and verifying an Audio Induction Loop Assistive Listening System (`AP-113`), how is the audio signal transmitted to the listener, and what must be verified across the seating area?
choices: Via line-of-sight infrared LEDs that are blocked by sunglasses
Via 60 GHz millimeter-wave Wi-Fi
Via unbalanced RCA cables plugged into each chair

A perimeter copper loop wire driven by a current amplifier generates a magnetic field that couples directly into a hearing aid's telecoil (T-coil); verify uniform magnetic field strength, frequency response, and low EMI hum across the seating area
explanation: An induction loop ALS uses a high-current loop amplifier and perimeter cable to create an alternating magnetic field picked up by hearing-aid T-coils; verification item AP-113 confirms end-to-end field uniformity and clarity.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 9, pp. 220-221; Chapter 14, p. 350

topic: Aspect Ratio Preservation (Pillarboxing and Letterboxing) on 16:9 Displays
prompt: When configuring a scaling presentation switcher to display legacy `4:3` (`1.33:1`) or wide CinemaScope `2.39:1` content on a native `16:9` (`1.77:1`) display, what is the standard calibration rule?
choices: Always preserve the content's original aspect ratio using black side bars (pillarboxing) or top/bottom bars (letterboxing) rather than stretching or distorting geometry, unless explicitly instructed otherwise by the client
Stretch all 4:3 images horizontally so people look 33% wider
Crop off the left and right edges of all 2.39:1 widescreen video
Rotate the image 90 degrees into portrait mode
explanation: Scalers must preserve the native aspect ratio of incoming content using pillarboxing or letterboxing rather than distorting circles into ovals or cropping critical content.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 15, p. 363

topic: Pythagorean Theorem Screen Diagonal Verification
prompt: During installation verification, an installer measures a projection screen's viewing area as `6 ft` (`1.83 m`) high and `8 ft` (`2.44 m`) wide. Using the Pythagorean theorem (`A² + B² = C²`), what is the exact diagonal size of the screen?
choices: 10 ft (3.05 m), because `sqrt(6² + 8²) = sqrt(36 + 64) = sqrt(100) = 10 ft`
explanation: By the Pythagorean theorem, Diagonal C = sqrt(Height² + Width²) = sqrt(6² + 8²) = sqrt(36 + 64) = sqrt(100) = 10 ft.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Appendix A, pp. 428-429

topic: Combined Ohm's Law and Power Law Voltage Verification (V = sqrt(P × R))
prompt: While verifying a test load, an installer drives `4 W` of continuous sine-wave power (`P = 4 W`) into a `16 Ω` loudspeaker load (`R = 16 Ω`). Using `V = sqrt(P × R)`, what RMS voltage should the multimeter read across the load?
choices: 4 V
8 V (`sqrt(4 W × 16 Ω) = sqrt(64) = 8 V`)
explanation: Combining Ohm's law (V = I × R) and the Power law (P = I × V) gives V = sqrt(P × R) = sqrt(4 × 16) = sqrt(64) = 8 V.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 2, pp. 24-27; Appendix A, p. 430

task: Demonstrate to Client that System Performs to Specifications
topic: Site Cleanup and Photographing Finished Room Before Client Walkthrough
prompt: Before inviting the client or consultant into the room for the closeout performance demonstration and sign-off, what mandatory site-preparation steps must the installation crew complete?
choices: Leave empty cardboard boxes stacked in the corner to prove new gear was used
Leave blue protective plastic film on all display bezels
Pile wire clippings under the conference table
Vacuum floors, dress all visible cables, wipe down racks and panels, remove protective films, restore moved furniture to its original layout, and photograph the finished room
explanation: A clean, finished site is an essential closeout deliverable; vacuuming, wiping down gear, restoring furniture, and photographing the completed installation must happen before the client walkthrough.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 16, pp. 379-381

task: Demonstrate to Client that System Performs to Specifications
topic: Empty Box and Refuse Disposal Rule on Client/GC Sites
prompt: During system closeout cleanup, what is the rule regarding how the AV crew disposes of empty equipment cardboard boxes, packing foam, and construction refuse?
choices: Always discard waste only where explicitly authorized by the general contractor/builder or client—or haul it back to your own shop if onsite disposal is not permitted
Dump all boxes into the nearest neighboring retail store's dumpster without asking
Stack all empty boxes in the client's fire exit stairwell
Burn cardboard packaging in the parking lot
explanation: Dumpster space on construction and client sites is tightly managed and billed; never dump boxes or refuse onsite without explicit GC/client authorization—haul it back to your shop if necessary.

task: Demonstrate to Client that System Performs to Specifications
topic: Safe Flat-Panel Display Cleaning Procedure Before Demonstration
prompt: While preparing a direct-view LCD/OLED flat panel for the client closeout demonstration, smudges are noticed on the screen. What is the correct cleaning procedure?
choices: Leave the display on at full brightness and spray ammonia glass cleaner directly onto the screen

Turn OFF the display (so smudges are visible and electronics are cool), wipe gently with a dry microfiber cloth (or dampen the cloth slightly with distilled water), and wipe in a single consistent vertical or horizontal direction
Scrub the screen in tight circles with a dry paper towel and rubbing alcohol
Use a razor blade scraper on the polarizer film
explanation: Always turn off the display first, never spray liquid directly onto the panel (where it runs behind the bezel into drivers), use a soft microfiber cloth dampened with distilled water if needed, and wipe in one consistent direction.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 16, pp. 382-383

task: Demonstrate to Client that System Performs to Specifications
topic: Projection Screen Surface Cleaning Direction (Bottom to Top)
prompt: If a front-projection screen surface gets dusty or smudged prior to closeout handover, how should it be cleaned according to Chapter 10 of the CTS-I Exam Guide?
choices: Spray lacquer thinner across the top and let it drip downward
Scrub horizontally with a stiff wire brush
Blot edges with a clean soft brush and gently wipe from bottom to top with mild water and a clean absorbent sponge (so dirty water never streaks down over dry fabric)
Remove the fabric and run it through a commercial washing machine
explanation: When cleaning a projection screen surface with mild water and a clean absorbent sponge, always work from bottom to top so runoff does not leave permanent vertical drip streaks on dry lower fabric.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 10, p. 249

task: Demonstrate to Client that System Performs to Specifications
topic: Substantial / Practical Completion (`DOC-110`) versus Final Acceptance (`DOC-120`)
prompt: Under ANSI/INFOCOMM 10:2013 (`DOC-110` and `DOC-120`), what is the difference between the 'Substantial / Practical Completion' milestone and the 'Final Acceptance' milestone?
choices: Substantial Completion happens before any cables are pulled; Final Acceptance happens during rough-in
There is no difference; both mean 50% of the racks are still in the warehouse
Final Acceptance comes first, followed 6 months later by Substantial Completion

Substantial / Practical Completion (`DOC-110`) is conditional owner sign-off that the system is ready for beneficial use (though minor punch-list items may remain), whereas Final Acceptance (`DOC-120`) confirms the project is 100% complete with all punch items and closeout deliverables satisfied
explanation: Substantial/Practical Completion (Phase 4 / DOC-110) grants conditional acceptance for beneficial use while minor punch list items are being closed; Final Acceptance (Phase 6 / DOC-120) signifies 100% completion of all project obligations.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 11, pp. 266-267; Chapter 16, pp. 384-386

task: Demonstrate to Client that System Performs to Specifications
topic: Punch / Snag List Resolution and Bringing Tools to the Walkthrough
prompt: What is a 'punch list' (or 'snag list') during system closeout, and why should the lead CTS-I bring hand tools, a label maker, connectors, and test gear to the client walkthrough?
choices: A checklist of minor incomplete or non-conforming physical, labeling, or functional items; bringing tools allows fixing quick items on the spot so they never hold up final acceptance and payment
A list of employees to be laid off after the project ends
A list of optional upgrades the sales team hopes to pitch next year
A structural calculation of concrete anchor hole depths
explanation: The punch/snag list records minor deficiencies that must be corrected to meet contract scope (and often gates final payment); bringing tools and labels to the walkthrough lets the installer resolve minor items immediately.

task: Demonstrate to Client that System Performs to Specifications
topic: Demonstrating Button-by-Button Control Conformance (`100–106`)

The approved button-by-button specification document (and quantitative latency metric under item 106)
The carpenter's millwork stain sample
An unapproved verbal wish list from a casual room user

task: Demonstrate to Client that System Performs to Specifications
topic: Volatile Organic Compounds (VOC) Monitoring During Installation and Closeout
prompt: When green-building or environmental stewardship compliance is verified at closeout, how are Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs) from onsite adhesives, sealants, paints, and aerosols quantified?

In candelas per square meter (nits)
In grams per liter (g/L) of product
In Rack Units (RU)

source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 16, p. 381

task: Demonstrate to Client that System Performs to Specifications
topic: Waste Diversion Tracking for Sustainable Project Closeout
prompt: In sustainable construction closeout reporting, what does the metric 'Waste Diversion' measure?
choices: The amount of audio signal diverted to an assistive listening loop
The percentage of network packets dropped by a firewall
The heat exhausted from the top of an equipment rack
The weight or volume of project waste materials diverted away from landfills through recycling, reuse, or manufacturer take-back programs

source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 16, p. 381

task: Demonstrate to Client that System Performs to Specifications
topic: Audio Coverage Uniformity Verification (`AP-114` / ANSI/AVIXA A102.01)
prompt: When demonstrating audio system performance to the consultant at closeout, which ANSI/AVIXA standard governs verification item `AP-114` for early-arriving sound pressure level uniformity across the listener area?

AVIXA F501.01:2015 (Cable Labeling)
ANSI/INFOCOMM V202.01:2016 (DISCAS)
ANSI/J-STD-710 (Drawing Symbols)
