source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 14, p. 350; Appendix B, p. 437

task: Demonstrate to Client that System Performs to Specifications
topic: Obtaining Formal Written Client Sign-Off Immediately After Demonstration/Training
prompt: When is the optimal moment for the lead CTS-I installer or project manager to obtain the client's or consultant's formal written acceptance sign-off?
choices: Six months after the crew has left the state
Right at or immediately following the successful system demonstration and user training session while all authorized stakeholders are present in the room
Before unpacking any equipment from the delivery truck
Never; verbal thumbs-up in the hallway is legally sufficient
explanation: Obtaining formal written sign-off immediately at the conclusion of the successful demonstration and training session—while the client's decision-makers are present and satisfied—prevents post-handover delays in billing and closeout.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 16, pp. 390-391

task: Demonstrate to Client that System Performs to Specifications
topic: Checking Secondary Ghost Reflections on Rear-Projection Mirrors
prompt: During the final visual quality check of a folded rear-projection system, the installer notices a faint, slightly larger 'ghost' duplicate image offset from the main picture. What causes this artifact?
choices: An incorrect IP subnet mask on the media server
A 60 Hz audio ground loop in the rack
Secondary reflection, where light bounces off the rear surface of the projection screen back onto the fold mirror and is reflected a second time onto the screen
Too much Kevlar yarn inside the fiber-optic cable
explanation: In folded rear-projection booths, secondary reflection occurs when projected light reflects off the back of the screen, hits the fold mirror again, and returns to the screen as a larger ghost image; slight geometry/angle adjustment resolves it.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 10, pp. 253-254

task: Provide Training on AV System Operation
topic: Critical Prohibition: Never Train Casual End Users to Change IP Addresses
prompt: When conducting closeout operation training for casual end users and presenters, which topic must NEVER be taught to general end users?
choices: How to turn the AV system on and off using the touch panel
How to switch presentation sources and adjust program volume
How to mute/unmute tabletop microphones and launch a video call
How to change device IP addresses, subnet masks, DSP gain structure, or system configuration settings (which must be restricted strictly to qualified technical staff)
explanation: Casual end users should be taught basic presentation operations (power on/off, source selection, conferencing, volume/mute, presets), and must NEVER be taught how to alter IP addresses or system configurations.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 16, pp. 388-390

task: Provide Training on AV System Operation
topic: Four Customer Training Audience Tiers
prompt: Why does AVIXA closeout best practice divide customer training into four distinct audience tiers (Technical Staff, Help Desk/Support Staff, Power Users, and Casual Users)?
choices: So each group receives training tailored to its specific operational role and technical depth—from deep IP/DSP diagnostics for Technical Staff to simple bullet-point quick-start guides for Casual Users
Because fire codes prohibit more than two people in a room during training
So the trainer can bill four times for reading the exact same manufacturer manual aloud
Because Casual Users are responsible for soldering replacement XLR cables
explanation: Tailoring training across the four audience tiers ensures technical staff master network/DSP maintenance, help-desk staff learn first-line user support, power users learn all operational modes, and casual users get clear, non-intimidating basics.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 16, pp. 388-390

task: Provide Training on AV System Operation
topic: Scheduling Training as a Dedicated Event with a Written Outline
prompt: How should customer training sessions be scheduled and structured to maximize user retention and minimize post-handover service calls?
choices: Give a 2-minute impromptu walkthrough while vacuuming the floor during punch-list work
Schedule training as a separate, dedicated event after installation and cleanup are finished, following a prepared written topic outline and providing concise operating guides
Email the 400-page C++ control compiler manual to the company CEO without meeting anyone
Conduct training in the noisy loading dock before the equipment is installed
explanation: Customer training should be scheduled as a dedicated, distraction-free session in the completed room using a written agenda/outline and role-appropriate quick-start documentation.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 16, pp. 388-389

task: Provide Training on AV System Operation
topic: Handling Out-of-Scope Feature Requests Raised During Training
prompt: Halfway through an end-user training session, an attendee asks why the 'Presentation' button doesn't also brew coffee and lower the hallway shades, and asks you to reprogram it right now. What is the correct response?
choices: Open the control code on your laptop and spend 4 hours rewriting the system for free
Tell the attendees that the system designer was incompetent
Explain that the system was programmed to the approved contract specification, note their request, and direct any desired feature additions to the Project Manager for a formal Change Order
Unplug the touch panel and end the training session immediately
explanation: Never reprogram a verified system on the spot during training or promise uncontracted features; log the client's wish-list item and route it to the Project Manager as a potential Change Order.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 16, p. 390

task: Provide Training on AV System Operation
topic: Training Help Desk Staff on 'Hand-Holding' First-Line Support

choices: Teaching them how to X-ray post-tension concrete slabs
Teaching them how to calculate conduit jam ratios
Teaching them how to re-cone blown subwoofers
Teaching them first-line symptom triage, basic verification checks, and how to calmly guide ('hand-hold') casual presenters through common operational questions
explanation: Help Desk training focuses on first-line triage and guiding ('hand-holding') casual users through everyday source switching, mute checks, and conference dialing—drastically reducing unnecessary service truck rolls.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 16, p. 389

task: Provide Training on AV System Operation
topic: Documenting Hidden Service Pages and PIN Codes for Technical Staff
prompt: During closeout training for the client's in-house Technical Staff tier, what specialized control-interface information obtained from the programmer must be shared and documented?
choices: The location, access sequence, and PIN codes for any hidden technician/service setup pages on the touch-panel GUI
The home phone numbers of the drywall crew
The wholesale distributor pricing of the HDMI cables
The chemical formula of the intumescent firestop putty
explanation: Control programmers often build hidden technician/service pages (protected by a button hold or PIN code) for routing diagnostics and startup overrides; these must be documented and taught to authorized technical staff.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 13, p. 317; Chapter 16, p. 389

task: Provide Training on AV System Operation
topic: Training Users on Wireless Microphone Battery Care and Mute Etiquette

Checking rechargeable battery status before sessions, keeping transmitters away from metal pockets/keys, muting when not speaking, and staying behind the front plane of the loudspeakers
Changing the receiver's UHF RF group and channel randomly before every meeting
Washing condenser microphone capsules in soapy water after each talker
explanation: Proper wireless mic training covers battery management, avoiding antenna shielding by hands or metal objects, muting unused mics, and staying behind the loudspeakers to avoid acoustic feedback.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 9, pp. 213-214; Chapter 16, p. 389

task: Provide Training on AV System Operation
topic: ANSI/INFOCOMM 4:2012 Energy Management User Training
prompt: Under ANSI/INFOCOMM 4:2012 (Audiovisual Systems Energy Management), how do user training and control automation work together to reduce ongoing facility power consumption?
choices: By training users to turn off the building's main fire-alarm panel every evening
By leaving all laser projectors and power amplifiers running 24/7/365
By combining automated occupancy/scheduled shutdown macros with user training on proper system power-down procedures at the end of meetings
By disconnecting the cooling fans inside the equipment rack
explanation: ANSI/INFOCOMM 4:2012 (and S601.01) achieves ongoing AV energy management through automated power-down schedules, consumption monitoring, and training users to shut down systems after use.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 1, p. 9; Appendix B, p. 437

task: Provide Training on AV System Operation
topic: Providing Concise Laminates / Quick-Start Guides at the Lectern

To cover up scratches on the conference table
To list the MAC addresses of all 32 HDCP repeaters
Because casual presenters rarely read thick technical manuals and need immediate, step-by-step visual instructions for starting a meeting, sharing content, and shutting down

source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 16, pp. 386, 389

task: Provide Training on AV System Operation
topic: Manual Power-Sequence Training When Sequencer Is Bypassed
prompt: If technical support staff must manually power up or power down an auditorium sound rack during maintenance when the automatic power sequencer is bypassed, what sequence must they be trained to follow?
choices: Power ON: Sources/Mixers/DSPs first, Power Amplifiers LAST; Power OFF: Power Amplifiers FIRST, wait 15 seconds, then turn off DSPs/Mixers/Sources
Power ON: Power Amplifiers first, then plug in microphones with +48V active; Power OFF: pull the main breaker under load
Turn all switches on and off simultaneously with a wooden broomstick
Leave the power amplifiers on while unplugging XLR inputs
explanation: Whenever powering audio racks manually, staff must turn amplifiers ON last and turn amplifiers OFF first (waiting 15 seconds before shutting down upstream electronics) to prevent speaker-destroying transient thumps.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 11, pp. 273-275

topic: Drawings of Record (As-Builts) Definition (`DOC-111` / `DOC-115`)
prompt: What are 'Drawings of Record' (As-Built Drawings) under ANSI/INFOCOMM 10:2013 closeout items `DOC-111` and `DOC-115`?
choices: The preliminary hand sketches drawn by the salesperson during the first client lunch
The final, updated architectural and AV system schematics reflecting every field modification, cable label ID, terminal assignment, and model substitution as actually installed
Generic marketing brochures downloaded from manufacturer websites
Unmarked floor plans from before the building was renovated
explanation: Drawings of Record (As-Builts) incorporate all field redlines—exact installed cable numbers, port assignments, mounting locations, and approved substitutions—to support future maintenance and upgrades.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 4, p. 74; Chapter 16, pp. 384-386

topic: Organizing Equipment Manuals in the Closeout Package (`DOC-117`)
prompt: According to Chapter 16 of the CTS-I Exam Guide, what is the best practice for organizing manufacturer equipment manuals in the closeout documentation binder (and where should a copy of operational documentation be kept)?
choices: Staple all manuals together in random order and mail them to the equipment manufacturer
Shred all manuals unless the client pays an extra storage fee

Arrange manuals in alphabetical order AND grouped by function (e.g., all audio manuals together, all display manuals together), and leave a copy of the operational documentation right with the AV equipment rack
Sort manuals by the weight of the paper and lock them in an off-site bank vault with no copy at the rack

topic: Backing Up DSP Configurations and Control Source/Compiled Code

So casual end users can edit the DSP crossover filters during meetings
Because the fire marshal inspects C# source code during fire drills

So that if a hardware processor fails or is reset years later, a technician can restore the exact verified calibration, routing, and control logic in minutes without re-engineering the room from scratch

topic: ANSI/AVIXA 10:2013 Wireless Frequency Licensing Permit (`DOC-103`)

That wireless transmitters are submerged in mineral oil
That all wireless microphones operate on the 2.4 GHz Bluetooth band
That wireless antennas are mounted inside a sealed steel safe

topic: Audio, Video, and Control Test Reports (`DOC-112`, `DOC-113`, `DOC-118`, `DOC-114`)

Completed Audio Test Report (`DOC-112`), Control Test Report (`DOC-113`), Video Test Report (`DOC-118`), and Final Commissioning Report (`DOC-114`)
Architectural concrete slump test reports and soil boring logs
Catering receipts from the kickoff meeting

topic: Warranty Activation and Transfer Documentation (`DOC-119`)

Keep all warranty certificates in an unmarked box in the installer's van
Register, activate, and formally transfer all manufacturer and integrator system warranties (with serial numbers and start/expiration dates) to the client
Tell the client that AV electronics never carry warranties

source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 16, pp. 385-387

topic: Recording Final Cable Label IDs on Drawings of Record (AVIXA F501.01)

So the client can count how many meters of tape were used
To satisfy the lighting designer's color Rendering Index
So any future maintenance technician can trace a cable's origin, destination, and signal type between the physical harness and the schematic without guessing or toning live bundles

source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, pp. 135-136; Chapter 16, p. 385

topic: Establishing the Site Maintenance Log at Handover
prompt: When handing over a completed fixed AV installation into ongoing support, what log document should be initialized and placed with the system documentation?

A blank checkbook signed by the project manager
A list of competitors' phone numbers
The architect's college transcript

source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 16, p. 387; Chapter 17, pp. 405-406

topic: Responsible Recycling When Client Declines Physical Paper Manuals (`DOC-117`)
prompt: If a client specifies digital PDF delivery of all user manuals under `DOC-117` and declines the hundreds of multilingual paper booklets packed inside the equipment boxes, what should the installer do with the paper manuals?
choices: Stuff the paper manuals inside the equipment rack blocking the cooling fans
Deliver the organized digital manuals per spec and responsibly recycle the unwanted paper booklets
Throw the paper manuals onto the drop-ceiling tiles
Refuse to hand over the digital PDFs unless the client takes the paper boxes

source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 16, pp. 381, 385

topic: Documenting Final Amplifier Attenuator and EQ Settings Against Tampering
prompt: After completing audio gain structure and room equalization, why should the technician record (or photograph) all physical amplifier attenuator positions and install security covers over front-panel knobs before closeout?
choices: Security covers increase the amplifier's output wattage by 3 dB
Photographing knobs automatically updates the DSP firmware
To document the verified baseline calibration in the closeout record and prevent unauthorized users from turning knobs and ruining gain structure or blowing speakers
To block cooling air from entering the front of the amplifier
explanation: Recording final attenuator/DSP settings in the closeout report and installing security covers/locks prevents casual tampering and allows instant restoration if settings are disturbed.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 14, pp. 336-337; Chapter 16, p. 386

topic: Transferring Final Network Device Inventory and Credentials to IT
prompt: At project closeout, why must the finalized Network Device Inventory—including as-installed MAC addresses, IP assignments, VLANs, open TCP/UDP ports,firmware versions, and administrative credentials—be formally handed over to the client's IT department?

Because MAC addresses are required to calculate room reverberation time
So IT can publish the admin passwords on the public company website
To support ongoing enterprise network monitoring, security auditing (RP-C303.01), firmware lifecycle management, and rapid hardware replacement
explanation: Handing over the verified Network Device Inventory and updated credentials at closeout enables the client's IT team to maintain cybersecurity, monitor uptime, and swap failed units seamlessly.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 12, pp. 285-287; Chapter 16, pp. 385-387

topic: Project Completion Definition (Not Complete Until Closeout Finishes)
prompt: According to Chapter 3 and Chapter 16 of the CTS-I Exam Guide, at what point is an audiovisual installation project officially considered complete?
choices: Only after all System Closeout activities—site cleanup, Drawings of Record/documentation handover, punch-list resolution, customer training, and formal client sign-off (`DOC-120`)—are 100% finished
As soon as the last rack screw is tightened in the shop
As soon as the projector turns on for the first time
When the initial sales deposit check clears
explanation: An AV project is not complete when the hardware is mounted or even when verification tests pass; it is complete only when System Closeout (cleanup, documentation, training, and final acceptance sign-off) is finished.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 3, p. 49; Chapter 16, pp. 379, 385

topic: Documenting Preventive Maintenance Schedules Based on Usage and Environment
prompt: When preparing the recommended Preventive Maintenance (PM) schedule in the closeout binder, which three factors determine how frequently each component must be serviced?
choices: The color of the rack paint, the length of the HDMI cables, and the brand of cage nuts
Expected hours of use, type of use, and the physical operating environment (such as dust, kitchen grease, high foot traffic, or theatrical fog/haze)
The alphabetical order of the manufacturer's name
The phase angle of the 70V speaker transformers
explanation: Preventive maintenance intervals are driven by hours of operation, type of usage, and environmental stressors such as dust, grease, or theatrical smoke/haze.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 16, p. 387; Chapter 17, pp. 401-403

topic: ISO/IEC 17024 CTS-I Credential Renewal Continuing Education (30 RUs)
prompt: After passing the CTS-I exam and closing out projects, how often must a certified installer renew the CTS-I credential under ANSI/ISO/IEC 17024 rules, and how many Renewal Units (RUs) of continuing education are required?
choices: Every 10 years with 5 Renewal Units
Never; CTS-I is a lifetime credential requiring no continuing education
Every 3 years by earning 30 Renewal Units (RUs) of approved continuing education and maintaining adherence to the CTS Code of Ethics and Conduct
Every 6 months by retaking the 150-minute written exam
explanation: Under ISO/IEC 17024 accreditation, CTS-I certification must be renewed every 3 years by completing 30 Renewal Units (RUs) and upholding the CTS Code of Ethics and Conduct.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 1, pp. 6-8

topic: Preventive Maintenance Definition versus Operational Tasks
prompt: Which activity is an operational task rather than a scheduled Preventive Maintenance (PM) activity?
choices: Cleaning projector intake air filters and heatsinks at fixed 500-hour intervals
Performing a scheduled mains-power pull test on the rack UPS battery backup
Checking audio system gain structure and room equalization calibration every 6 months
Changing the preset operating frequencies on handheld event radios for an incoming rental show
explanation: Preventive maintenance inspects, cleans, calibrates, and tests equipment at fixed intervals regardless of current condition; reconfiguring radio channel presets for a show is an operational setup task, not PM.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 17, pp. 401-405, 411

topic: Harsh Environments Requiring Accelerated Air Filter Maintenance
prompt: In which operating environments must active cooling air-intake filters on projectors, amplifiers, and racks be cleaned or replaced much more frequently than standard office schedules?
choices: High pedestrian traffic areas, commercial kitchens (grease vapors), chalkboard classrooms, smoking venues, and stages using theatrical fog, haze, smoke, or pyrotechnics
Clean-room semiconductor laboratories with positive HEPA filtration
Unoccupied dark storage vaults
Passive loudspeaker cabinets with no fans or vents
explanation: Airborne dust from heavy foot traffic or chalk, kitchen grease, smoke, and glycol/oil residue from theatrical fog and haze machines rapidly clog intake filters and coat heatsinks, requiring accelerated PM intervals.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 17, pp. 401-402

topic: Detecting Early Fan and Color-Wheel Bearing Failure with an Electronic Stethoscope
prompt: Aside from cooling fans, what other high-speed rotating mechanical assemblies inside projectors are prone to motor bearing wear, and what tool can detect early bearing whine during preventive maintenance?
choices: LCD glass polarizers; tested with a 3-lamp outlet tester
Single-chip DLP RGB color wheels and laser-phosphor wheels; early bearing wear can be detected by listening carefully or using an electronic stethoscope
Passive Fresnel lenses; tested with an OTDR
HDMI connectors; tested with a plumb bob
explanation: Cooling fans, single-DLP color wheels, and laser-phosphor wheels are high-speed rotating parts whose motor bearings wear over time; listening with an electronic stethoscope catches bearing noise before seizure and thermal shutdown.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 17, pp. 402-403

topic: Controlled Mains-Power Pull Test for UPS Battery Verification
prompt: During a scheduled preventive maintenance visit, why is checking the green front-panel status LED on a rack UPS insufficient, and what test should be performed (during an approved maintenance window)?
choices: Short the UPS output terminals with a screwdriver to test the breaker
Submerge the sealed lead-acid battery in distilled water
Perform a controlled mains-power pull test (unplugging or tripping the feed breaker) to verify that the UPS batteries actually hold the live AV rack load for the specified runtime
Connect the UPS output to the 70V loudspeaker bus
explanation: Aged UPS batteries often show 'full charge' under zero load but collapse immediately when AC mains drops; a scheduled mains-power pull test proves the UPS holds the actual rack load.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 17, p. 403

topic: Simulating Controlled Faults to Verify Redundant Failover Systems
prompt: How should a maintenance technician verify a mission-critical AV system equipped with automatic failover switches and hot-standby backup processors/amplifiers?
choices: Assume the backup unit works as long as its power light is on
Unplug the backup unit and take it home as warehouse stock
Never test failover until the primary unit catches fire during a live broadcast
Deliberately simulate a controlled fault event on the primary unit during a maintenance window to prove the hot-standby unit takes over seamlessly, and periodically rotate active/standby roles
explanation: Redundant failover systems must be verified during PM visits by triggering a controlled primary fault to confirm seamless switchover, and active/standby units should be rotated to equalize wear.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 17, pp. 404-405

topic: In-House Master Reference Calibration for Technician Multimeters
prompt: What is the AVIXA-recommended, cost-effective method for keeping every field technician's toolbox multimeter and test meters accurately calibrated?
choices: Maintain laboratory-certified calibration on a single high-precision master reference instrument in-house, and regularly calibrate technicians' field meters against that master reference
Ship every technician's multimeter to a national metrology lab every week
Never calibrate field multimeters as long as the battery icon is not flashing
Adjust the multimeter calibration screws randomly until it reads 100 V on a 9 V battery
explanation: Sending every field meter to an accredited lab is costly and causes downtime; organizations should maintain lab certification on one master reference instrument and calibrate field meters against it in-house.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 17, pp. 407-408, 411

topic: Maintaining Sharp Cutting/Stripping Tools and Safety Tagging Power Tools
prompt: Why must dull utility-knife blades, wire strippers, and drill bits be sharpened or replaced immediately, and what periodic compliance check applies to mains-powered hand tools on job sites?
choices: Dull blades cut faster through Kevlar fiber

Dull blades require excessive force and skip/jump dangerously (causing lacerations), while mains-powered tools require intact guards, ground pins, and periodic electrical safety testing and tagging (PAT tags)
Safety guards on circular saws should be wired open during maintenance
Mains-powered drills should have their ground pins clipped off
explanation: Sharp tools cut cleanly and safely without slipping, and mains-powered tools must maintain intact safety guards and current electrical safety inspection tags.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 17, pp. 406-407

topic: Inspecting High-Cycle User-Facing BYOD Patch Cables
prompt: Why should user-facing tabletop HDMI, USB-C, and 3.5 mm patch cables be inspected and continuity-tested on every preventive maintenance visit?
choices: Because copper cables evaporate when exposed to fluorescent light
Because tabletop cables are immune to physical wear
Because consumer/prosumer AV connectors are rated for only a few thousand (or fewer) mate/unmate cycles and suffer strained pins, bent shells, and broken shields from daily user handling
Because replacing a patch cord requires a structural engineer's stamp
explanation: User-facing connectivity cables endure constant flexing, yanking, and mate/unmate wear (often rated for only a few thousand cycles) and are the #1 source of intermittent room faults.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 17, pp. 403-404

topic: Firmware Update Policy and Scheduled Processor Reboots During PM
prompt: When performing software/firmware maintenance on a stable, mission-critical control or DSP system, what policy consideration and routine action should the technician follow?
choices: Install untested beta firmware five minutes before a board of directors meeting
Never reboot any processor until its memory overflows and crashes
Delete the backup configuration file before updating firmware

Follow the agreed client policy (balancing 'if it ain't broke, don't fix it' stability against critical security patches), back up running configs first, and include scheduled periodic reboots to clear memory leaks
explanation: Firmware updates should follow a clear client policy with full pre-update backups, and continuously running processors benefit from scheduled periodic reboots to maintain clean memory states.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 17, p. 404

topic: Xenon Arc Lamp Protective Equipment (PPE) During Replacement
prompt: When servicing a large-venue cinema or auditorium projector equipped with a high-pressure Xenon arc lamp, why must the technician wear a full polycarbonate face shield, leather gauntlets, and a heavy protective jacket?
choices: Xenon lamps contain gas under extreme internal pressure even when cold and can shatter explosively if dropped, scratched, or stressed during handling
Xenon lamps emit loud 140 dB SPL acoustic tones when unplugged
The protective jacket prevents static electricity from changing the screen aspect ratio
Xenon lamps are filled with liquid acid that drips from the BNC jacks
explanation: Xenon arc lamps operate under extreme internal gas pressure and present a severe explosion/shrapnel hazard when handled; full face shield, gauntlets, and body protection are mandatory.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 10, p. 244; Chapter 17, p. 403

topic: OLED Blue-Subpixel Luminance Degradation Over Lifespan
prompt: When inspecting aging direct-view OLED displays during a maintenance audit, which color channel degrades fastest over thousands of operating hours, shifting the display's white balance?
choices: Infrared
Shorter-wavelength Blue organic compounds degrade faster than Red and Green ('blue fading')
Green degrades within 10 hours while Blue lasts 100 years
Black pixels turn into mirrors
explanation: In organic light-emitting diode (OLED) panels, the shorter-wavelength blue emissive organic material has a shorter operational lifespan and degrades faster than red and green.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 10, p. 246

topic: Maintaining Ceiling Projector Alignment Without Digital Keystone Shortcuts
prompt: During a semi-annual maintenance check, a ceiling-mounted projector's image has drifted slightly off the screen border. What is the proper maintenance procedure?
choices: Apply 15 degrees of electronic keystone correction from the handheld remote and leave
Move the projection screen 300 mm to the right without telling the client

Inspect the structural mount, pipe threads, and setscrews for looseness or vibration, mechanically realign and lock the mount, verify optical focus/geometry, and record the work in the Maintenance Log
Zoom the lens smaller so a 500 mm black gap surrounds the image
explanation: Image drift indicates mechanical movement or loose hardware; always inspect the mount and setscrews for safety, realign mechanically/optically (never masking a loose mount with digital keystone), and log the action.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 10, pp. 256-258; Chapter 17, pp. 405-406

topic: Four Mandatory Pre-Troubleshooting Preparation Steps
prompt: Before traveling to a site and touching a malfunctioning AV system, what four preparation steps must a repair technician complete?
choices: Order a brand-new rack, cancel the client's warranty, erase the DSP code, and leave test meters at the shop
Call the fire department, shut off the building water main, evacuate the floor, and cut the feeder conduit
Promise the client the repair is free, bring only a pocketknife, skip reading the schematics, and guess which part failed
Familiarize yourself with the system design/operation, obtain the Drawings of Record/documentation, bring the proper toolkit and spares, and verify the warranty and maintenance agreement terms
explanation: Effective repair starts before touching the rack: review system operation, gather as-built documentation and configs, pack test tools and spares, and confirm warranty/service-contract coverage.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 17, pp. 396-398

topic: Number-One Cause of Electronic System Failures (Faulty Connections)
prompt: According to the troubleshooting principles in Chapters 11 and 17 of the CTS-I Exam Guide, what is the single most common cause of hardware faults in audiovisual systems, and what is the Golden Rule when testing changes?
choices: The majority of problems are caused by faulty cable connections (loose, unplugged, or mis-wired connectors); assume nothing, change only ONE thing at a time, and if it doesn't fix the fault, change it back before testing the next item
Cosmic radiation flipping DSP memory bits; change five settings at once to save time
Defective copper ore from the mine; replace all rack processors before checking power cords
Loudspeaker magnets losing magnetism overnight; never document what you changed
explanation: Most electronic system faults trace back to simple connection issues; technicians must make zero assumptions and change only one variable at a time—reverting any change that does not solve the problem.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 11, p. 278; Chapter 17, pp. 398-399

topic: Divide and Conquer (Half-Splitting) Fault Isolation Strategy
prompt: An auditorium audio chain (`Wireless Mic → Receiver → Mixer → DSP → Crossover → Power Amp → Loudspeaker`) has no output. To isolate the fault in the fewest steps using 'Divide and Conquer' (Half-Splitting), where should the technician test first?
choices: Unsolder the voice coil inside the ceiling loudspeaker first

Split the signal chain near the accessible midpoint (e.g., checking meters or injecting/monitoring signal at the Mixer/DSP interface) to immediately eliminate half of the system, then bisect the failing half
Replace every piece of equipment from left to right starting with the microphone capsule
Rewrite the touch-panel GUI graphics
explanation: Divide and Conquer (Half-Splitting) tests at the midpoint of a signal chain: if signal is normal at the midpoint, the fault is downstream; if absent, the fault is upstream—halving the search space on each test.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 11, pp. 279-280; Chapter 17, pp. 399-400

topic: Midpoint Cross-Plugging (Channel Swapping) Diagnostic Interpretation
prompt: Channel 1 of a stereo system is dead while Channel 2 works normally. At the midpoint between the mixer output and power amplifier input, you cross-plug Mixer Out 1 into Amp In 2, and Mixer Out 2 into Amp In 1. Now Speaker 1 plays normally and Speaker 2 is dead. Where is the fault?
choices: Downstream in Power Amplifier Channel 1 or Loudspeaker 1
In the AC mains circuit breaker feeding the rack
Upstream in Mixer Channel 1 (because the fault moved from Output 1 to Output 2 when the upstream feeds were swapped at the midpoint)
In the room's acoustic reverberation time
explanation: When cross-plugging at a midpoint, if the dead channel moves to the other side, the fault is upstream (before the cross-plug); if the dead channel stays on the same speaker, the fault is downstream.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 11, pp. 279-280

topic: Eliminating 50/60 Hz Ground-Loop Hum Safely Without Lifting Mains Earth
prompt: After replacing a line-level source device in a lectern that feeds a distant rack mixer, a loud 60 Hz ground-loop hum appears on the audio channel. Which repair action safely eliminates the ground loop?
choices: Snap off the third (earth ground) prong on the lectern device's AC power cord
Install a 3-prong-to-2-prong cheater plug on the rack power amplifier
Disconnect the green safety ground wire inside the building breaker panel

Insert a 1:1 audio isolation transformer (or DI box with ground lift) in the balanced audio signal path—or disconnect the audio cable shield at the receiving (load) end only—while keeping all AC mains safety earth grounds 100% intact
explanation: Never defeat an AC mains safety earth ground (which creates a lethal shock hazard); break audio ground loops in the signal path using an audio isolation transformer or by lifting the audio shield at the receiving end only.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 8, pp. 195-196; Chapter 11, pp. 271, 276

topic: Diagnosing Cheap HDMI Distribution Amplifier HDCP Key Exhaustion
prompt: A Blu-ray player works perfectly when plugged directly into Display 1, Display 2, or Display 3 individually, but all three displays go blank or show snow when fed simultaneously through a low-cost 1×4 HDMI Distribution Amplifier (DA). What is the root cause?
choices: The inexpensive HDMI DA fails to manage HDCP repeater authentication and exhausts the source device's limited HDCP key count across multiple sinks; replace it with an HDCP-compliant repeater/DA with EDID/HDCP management
Blu-ray players can only output analog composite video
The displays need their contrast ratios reduced below 7:1
The room's ambient noise exceeds 35 dBA
explanation: When a source works directly with each sink but fails through a splitter/DA, the DA is failing to manage EDID or HDCP key/repeater authentication across multiple downstream sinks.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 10, p. 242; Chapter 15, pp. 357-358

topic: Systematic RS-232 Serial Control Fault Isolation Before Calling Programmer
prompt: A rack processor's RS-232 port stops controlling a display after a technician re-dressed the rear rack cables. What four hardware/configuration checks must the technician verify BEFORE calling the control programmer?
choices: Only check whether the projector lens cap is on

Verify (1) cable is plugged into the correct control port, (2) TX/RX/GND pinout and continuity (no broken/shorted wires from tight ties), (3) baud rate/parity/data/stop bits match the manual, and (4) the display's control port is enabled in its setup menu
Delete the compiled control program and factory-reset the enterprise router
Replace the display with a different brand immediately
explanation: Before escalating to a control programmer, always verify port assignment, physical cable pinout/continuity (TX/RX/GND), serial parameters (baud, parity, data/stop bits), and device menu standby/control settings.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 13, pp. 319-320

topic: Diagnosing Non-Minimum Phase Acoustic Cancellation (Single vs. Multiple Locations)
prompt: While troubleshooting a frequency-response dip in an auditorium, adjusting the DSP parametric equalizer produces zero acoustic change on the analyzer. How do you determine whether the root cause is a loudspeaker crossover/driver fault versus a room reflection?
choices: Turn the equalizer boost up to +24 dB until the woofer smokes
Check the IP address of the equalizer

Measure at multiple locations: if the non-minimum-phase anomaly appears at MULTIPLE locations, it is a loudspeaker driver/crossover alignment issue; if it appears at ONE location only, it is a local room reflection
Replace the omnidirectional measurement mic with a piezo tweeter
explanation: When an EQ filter produces no acoustic change, the dip is a phase cancellation: if present across multiple seat locations, the cause is crossover/multi-driver interference; if localized to one spot, it is an architectural reflection.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 14, pp. 348-349

topic: Tracing Unlabeled Copper Cables with an Inductive Tone Generator and Probe
prompt: During a repair visit to an older facility that lacks as-built drawings or cable labels, how should the technician identify which twisted-pair cable in a rack bundle runs to a specific wall plate?
choices: Connect 120 V AC mains power to the wall plate and see which rack cable sparks
Cut every cable in the rack bundle one by one until the room goes dead
Use an Optical Time-Domain Reflectometer (OTDR) on the copper wire

Disconnect the cable from active electronics, attach an audio/RF tone generator ('fox') to the pair at the wall plate, and trace the signal inductively at the rack using a handheld inductive amplifier probe ('hound')
explanation: A two-piece tone generator and inductive probe ('fox and hound') injects a harmless tone onto an unenergized copper pair so the matching cable can be identified inductively inside a bundle without stripping insulation.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 12, p. 305

topic: Step 3 Failure Analysis: Preventing Repeat System Failures
prompt: In the 3-step troubleshooting methodology (Step 1: Symptom Recognition; Step 2: Localize Faulty Function; Step 3: Analysis & Root-Cause Prevention), what must the technician determine after repairing the immediate hardware fault?
choices: Perform failure analysis to determine why the failure occurred—such as inadequate user training, missing preventive maintenance, poor ventilation, or improper component selection—and log corrective recommendations so it does not recur
Close the ticket without writing anything in the Maintenance Log
Blame the end user in writing without checking the rack temperature
Disable all system error logs
explanation: Step 3 of systematic troubleshooting requires root-cause failure analysis (evaluating whether training, PM schedules, cooling, or component selection caused the breakdown) and updating the Maintenance Log to prevent repeat failures.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 11, pp. 280-281; Chapter 17, pp. 405-406

topic: Diagnosing PC Fallback Resolution versus Media Player Black Screen on EDID Loss
prompt: In a dual-source room, a presenter's laptop displays an image at a wrong, low 4:3 resolution while a dedicated Blu-ray/media player outputs a completely black screen (`0 V` video). Which single signal failure explains both symptoms simultaneously?
choices: The room's acoustic ambient noise is too high

An EDID / +5V Hot Plug Detect (HPD) communication failure between the display/switcher and the sources (causing the PC to fall back to a default safe resolution while the dedicated AV source shuts off its output)
The loudspeaker line has a 70V transformer tap mismatch
The projector's throw ratio is too long
explanation: When EDID or +5V HPD fails, computers typically fall back to a low default resolution, whereas dedicated AV sources (media players, cameras) often output no video at all or drop to 480p.
source: Official CTS-I Exam Guide, 2nd ed., Chapter 15, pp. 354-356

topic: Diagnosing Backward-Wired 70V Loudspeaker Step-Down Transformer
prompt: After a facility handyman replaces a single ceiling speaker on a 70.7 V distributed paging line, the paging amplifier immediately trips its over-current protection fault. Sweeping the disconnected line with a `Z`-meter shows near-zero impedance. What mistake did the handyman likely make?
choices: He set the speaker transformer tap to 2.5 W instead of 5 W
He left the ceiling speaker unplugged in the box

He wired the 70V step-down transformer backward—connecting the 8-ohm voice-coil secondary leads to the 70V trunk line (turning it into a step-up short circuit)—or connected an 8-ohm speaker directly across the 70V line without a transformer
